items.title: Yorks & Lincs Summer Fun Day
items.snippet: FCA foster families from across Yorkshire and Lincolnshire came together for a fantastic summer fun day packed with activities, food, friendship and plenty of smiles. The post Yorks & Lincs Summer Fun Day appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
A Fantastic Summer Event

Foster families from across our Yorkshire and Lincolnshire regions came together for a fun-filled summer day at Mansfield FC, enjoying activities, food and time together as a fostering community.

The weather was just right; after the recent heatwaves, we had a warm, dry day, meaning all our families were able to enjoy an activity packed day, both outdoors and indoors.

Fun for Everyone

Outdoor activities included an inflatable play centre for the toddlers, larger inflatable bouncy castle for the older children, climbing wall, football activities and races too!

Indoors there was an air hockey table, dance machine, craft/arts and tattoo station.

There was also a dedicated quiet and sensory area, with cushions and throws available for anyone who wanted to take a break from the excitement and enjoy some calmer time.

After exerting so much energy, a lunch of pizza and potato wedges went down a treat (with old and young alike!) followed by ice-cream and ice lollies, provided by an on-site ice-cream van, which was extremely popular with everyone!

Here are some of the comments received during the day –

“Our young person has made lots of friends and really enjoyed it”.

“The climbing wall was brilliant”.

Bringing our Fostering Community Together

We had a fantastic turn out for this event, from across the regions, and we got to see a lot of happy faces – children and foster parents too.

Events like these are such a wonderful opportunity for our foster parents and children to meet with others who understand fostering, enjoy time together and build life-long friendships.

As well as creating plenty of memories, our wonderful foster families also helped raise £71 for Cancer Research UK through the tombola. A huge thank you to everyone who contributed and helped make the day such a success!

items.title: TACT Lobby For Free School Meals For Children-In-Care
items.snippet: TACT have joined forces with The Fostering Network to lobby the Department for Education for free school meals for children-in-care. The post TACT Lobby For Free School Meals For Children-In-Care appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT Lobby For Free School Meals For Children-In-Care

TACT have joined forces with The Fostering Network to lobby the Department for Education (DfE) to extend free school meals entitlement to all children in foster care.

In June 2025, the government announced that, from the 2026 to 2027 academic year, the eligibility criteria for free school meals in England would be expanded to all children in households receiving Universal Credit. Whilst this was a welcomed decision for those households, a significant number of young people in foster care would not be eligible for those free school meals.

TACT immediately joined forces with The Fostering Network and approached the Department for Education (DfE). They agreed to co-design a survey that The Fostering Network would share with all members. The survey closed on Sunday 9th August and it had a huge response, with 713 foster carers in England completing the survey, highlighting the importance of this issue.

There were some significant key findings.

51% of foster carers stated that the children they foster are expected to lose their free school meal entitlement from September 2026, despite living in low-income households – as carers are unable to claim Universal Credit due to savings exceeding eligibility thresholds, often set aside for retirement or used to meet the needs of children in their care. The survey also found that household incomes were only slightly above the eligibility threshold, and that some were ineligible for Universal Credit due to being above State Pension age.

A number of foster carers highlighted significant financial concerns, with many estimating that the loss of free school meals would increase costs by more than £100 per child per month. This was a particular concern for foster carers with 3+ children all currently on free school meals. With fostering allowances not universally increasing to offset these costs, carers reported that they may need to reduce spending on other essentials, including clothing and/or activities for children.

There was strong support for automatic free school meals entitlement for all children-in-care, regardless of their foster carer’s income or benefit status. Many carers reported that free school meals provided continuity, stability and routine for children. This was seen as particularly important during transitions, such as moving between foster families or reunification with birth families. Many also cited the local authority’s role as corporate parent, arguing that children-in-care should automatically qualify for free school meals.

Foster carers also expressed considerable concerns about the wider implications of losing free school meals entitlement, particularly the potential loss of access to the Holiday Activities and Food (HAF) programme. As HAF eligibility is linked to benefits-related free school meals, children-in-care who lose their entitlement may also lose access to holiday activities, food provision and opportunities for social engagement.

The survey results are now with the DfE and TACT are lobbying them to extend free school meals entitlement to all children in foster care.

The post TACT Lobby For Free School Meals For Children-In-Care appeared first on TACT.

items.title: In a recent post, we introduced PACE: Playfulness, Acceptance, Curiosity and Empathy - and explored what P, for Playfulness, mea...
items.snippet: In a recent post, we introduced PACE: Playfulness, Acceptance, Curiosity and Empathy - and explored what P, for Playfulness, means in fostering. (Feed generated with FetchRSS)
items.content:
In a recent post, we introduced PACE: Playfulness, Acceptance, Curiosity and Empathy - and explored what P, for Playfulness, means in fostering.

Now it’s time for A – Acceptance.

Acceptance is about accepting a child for who they are, without judgement. It means recognising and validating their feelings, experiences and behaviours, helping them to feel safe, valued and understood.

You might not always agree with how a child sees a situation, or how they express themselves, but accepting their feelings doesn’t mean agreeing with them. It means showing them that it’s okay to feel the way they do.

For example, if a child says, “Everyone hates me,” it can be tempting to respond with, “That’s not true!” Instead, a PACE approach might be: “I’m sorry you feel like everyone hates you. That must be really upsetting.”

By responding with understanding rather than trying to change how they feel, we can help children feel heard, understood and less alone. 💛

Because sometimes, understanding the child behind the behaviour is where the biggest difference begins.

If you haven’t done so already, take a look at Michelle Newman-Brown’s blog, which explains PACE and Acceptance in more detail: https://ow.ly/WkXF50ZBQAw

#Fostering #PACE #Acceptance #FosterCare #TherapeuticParenting

TACT North West Rated Outstanding by Ofsted For Second Time
items.snippet: TACT's North West region has achieved an 'outstanding' rating by OFSTED for a second consecutive inspection. The post TACT North West Rated Outstanding by Ofsted For Second Time appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT North West Rated Outstanding by Ofsted For Second Time

TACT’s North West fostering service has been rated outstanding by Ofsted for the second consecutive inspection, reaffirming the exceptional support provided to children, young people and foster carers across the region.

Inspectors awarded the service the highest possible rating for:

  • Overall experiences and progress of children and young people
  • How well children and young people are helped and protected
  • The effectiveness of leaders and managers

The report highlighted the ‘exceptional care’ provided to children living with TACT foster families, noting that children develop trust, confidence and a strong sense of belonging, while benefiting from stable and nurturing homes.

Ofsted also praised the service’s strong safeguarding practice, ambitious leadership and child-centred cultures, as well as TACT’s commitment to helping children achieve positive outcomes in education, emotional wellbeing and long-term stability.

Ramona Catarig, Operational Director of Children’s Services for the North, said: “We are incredibly proud of this outstanding judgement. It reflects our unwavering commitment to the children and young people we support, our foster carers, and our partners, as well as our dedication to continuous learning and improvement. Above all, it demonstrates our determination to ensure that every child has the opportunity to thrive.

“This achievement reflects the dedication of our foster carers and colleagues, who work tirelessly to ensure children experience the stability, love and support they deserve. Most importantly, it recognises the resilience, progress and achievements of the children and young people we are privileged to support every day.

“As we look ahead, we remain focused on building on this success, listening to the voices of children and foster carers, and delivering the highest quality care and support.”

The inspection took place in June 2026 and found that children consistently feel safe, valued and part of their foster families, with leadership described as inspirational and practice as reflective and child focused.

Read TACT North West’s OFSTED report.

The post TACT North West Rated Outstanding by Ofsted For Second Time appeared first on TACT.

items.title: Making Memories At Outdoor Residential
items.snippet: TACT Scotland took a group of young people and foster carers on an unforgettable outdoor residential trip to Broomlee Outdoor Education Centre The post Making Memories At Outdoor Residential appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Making Memories At Outdoor Residential

Our TACT Scotland Team took a group of young people on an outdoor residential, providing a fantastic opportunity for them to grow in confidence, develop new skills and support one another through shared outdoor experiences.

The residential took place at Broomlee Outdoor Education Centre, on the outskirts of the conservation village of West Linton. During the visit, we had a total of 22 people attend including children and staff. 16  young people from 9 different families took part in a variety of activities that focused on team building, communication and peer support. These activities included two separate high rope tasks, fire building, evening games and night line.

Both high rope activities were a big hit with our young people, including the Leap of Faith, which focused on confidence building and bravery. Here the young people would climb an 8 metre high pole, stand on top and then leap off to hit a target buoy. This was a difficult challenge, but it was incredible to see the bravery of the young people taking part, and how they attempted to go higher on their second attempt and push their limits a little further. It was great to see them encouraging each other from below and congratulating each other on their jump.

Crate stack, the other high rope activity, was a great team builder – as it focused on one team member standing on stacked crates to try and get as high as they could without falling, whilst their team mates supported by placing each crate on once the climber was ready.   

Another great activity for communication was night line, where the whole team was blindfolded, and they had to follow the line over, under and around the obstacles to complete the course. For this activity it was essential for the young people to clearly communicate in order for the people behind them to prepare to overcome the obstacle in front of them.

There were many highlights of this trip including seeing the young people overcome their fears and building their confidence, as well as witnessing the peer support as they did so. For some, it was their first ever residential and it was nice to see them navigate this new experience and enjoy themselves. 

Feedback from our young people and foster carers was unanimously positive. One young person said that he loved the range of activities and spending time with others; it helped him to develop a bit more self confidence when meeting new people, and taking part in unfamiliar activities. He said that he wished it was longer!

A TACT foster carer said: “What an honour it was to be in the company of our amazing children and young people at camp.  They barely knew each other or some of the adults.  Yet, they were resilient, supportive, inclusive, and empathetic throughout the two days and were a credit to their carers, and the wider TACT support network around them.”

A big ‘thank you’ to our team for organising such an enjoyable and enriching event, that everyone clearly enjoyed!

The post Making Memories At Outdoor Residential appeared first on TACT.

How one decision became a family journey in fostering
items.snippet: Jamila and Shakila are sisters from the West Midlands who share a passion for fostering. With over 20 years of experience between them, they reflect on how fostering became part of their family life, the support they’ve received from FCA, and the everyday moments that make caring for children so rewarding. The post How one decision became a family journey in fostering appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
Jamila and Shakila’s Fostering Story

Jamila and Shakila are sisters based in the West Midlands who share a deep commitment to fostering. Shakila has been fostering for 15 years, while Jamila has been fostering for 6 years, and together they have supported a number of children, including sibling groups.

For them, fostering isn’t just something they do – it has become part of their family life, shaped by shared experiences, support, and a commitment to helping children feel safe and valued.

Deciding to foster

For Shakila, fostering was something she had thought about for a long time before taking the first step.

“We were thinking about it…once the children were old enough to understand what fostering is, we then we took the step and we’ve just never looked back.”

Over time, her experience inspired her sister Jamila, who had already been supporting her as part of a wider family network and had a professional background in education.

“Jamila was interested in fostering from the very beginning, she just has a love for children.”

When the opportunity finally came, Jamila didn’t hesitate: “Fostering felt like something I really wanted to do, so I saved up to move into a larger home with more space and I’ve been fostering ever since.”

Having seen fostering up close, she felt more confident taking that next step. “It was much less scary, because I already knew what it was like.”

Starting the journey

Like many people considering fostering, both sisters had questions at the beginning. But having access to real experiences and honest conversations helped them feel reassured in their decision.

They emphasise how important it is to speak to people who understand fostering first-hand, as it gives a clearer and more realistic picture of what to expect – both the positives and the challenges.

Are you thinking of fostering?

Download the FCA’s complete beginner’s guide to fostering a child. Find out more on how to foster a child and the process involved.

Download Guide

The difference of fostering with FCA

For Jamila and Shakila, having the right support around them has made all the difference.

“FCA have always been supportive, they always ask, ‘What do you need?’”

They both highlight how important it is to feel part of a wider network of carers and professionals. “It’s nice to talk to other carers and realise, okay – this is normal.”

Knowing that help is always available brings reassurance, particularly during more challenging moments. “There’s always someone there for you – you’re not on your own.”

If you’re thinking about fostering and want to understand the support available, you can find out more here:

Understanding children’s needs

A key part of fostering is recognising that children’s behaviour often reflects their experiences. “There’s always a reason behind the behaviour.”

Both sisters emphasise the importance of empathy, patience and understanding, particularly when children are adjusting to a new environment. “You have to persevere and be emotionally strong.”

Over time, training and experience help carers understand how best to respond and support each child individually.

Jamila and Shakila are open about the fact that fostering can be challenging at times, but they also emphasise that challenges are a natural part of caring for any child. “You’re going to get challenges, but don’t you get challenges with your own children?”

They encourage others to approach challenges with patience and to make use of the support available. “You work with the child, understand what’s happening, and there’s support.”

Their perspective helps normalise the ups and downs, reassuring others that they won’t face them alone.

A wider family approach

Over time, fostering has become something shared across their wider family, with other relatives also becoming involved. “It makes me feel happy – knowing more children are being supported.”

They believe that talking openly about fostering helps others feel more confident in taking that first step. “You have to be honest, tell people the reality and the support that’s there.”

By sharing their experiences, they’ve helped others see that fostering is something they could do too.

For both sisters, the most meaningful moments in fostering are often the smallest ones. “Sometimes it’s just sitting there and seeing happy, content children.”

They speak about the importance of everyday connection – the moments that show a child is beginning to feel safe, settled and part of a family. “You’ll find something rewarding every single day.”

These moments, whether big or small, are what make fostering so meaningful.

Thinking about fostering?

Jamila encourages people who are interested to seek out more information about fostering.

“My brother also became a foster parent and our mum and dad love being extra grandparents to these wonderful children. We’ve become a fostering family! I couldn’t recommend it enough.”

“I don’t think anyone would regret fostering, once they’ve taken that leap of faith.”

“Come join us.”

items.title: Understanding Why Some Babies Enter Foster Care at Birth
items.snippet: Some babies enter foster care as soon as they are born due to concerns about their safety and wellbeing. This guide explains why these decisions are made, how safeguarding processes work, and the different circumstances that can lead to a newborn being placed in care. The post Understanding Why Some Babies Enter Foster Care at Birth appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
If you’re thinking about fostering babies, it’s only natural to have questions about why they’re in care, rather than with their biological families. Children can enter care for a few reasons, but the most common are abuse and neglect.

Safeguarding decisions about where a child should live can happen at any point during their childhood if a concern about their welfare is raised. In some cases, they might happen before a child is even born.

Some babies will move into care alongside their siblings, whereas others may live in a foster home with a parent. And in rare cases, a newborn baby might be fostered on their own.

Join us as we take a closer look at why babies enter care at birth, how these decisions are made, and what this means for birth families.

Why babies enter care at birth

Social services will only remove a baby from their birth family as a last resort. In some circumstances, these choices are made before the child is born as part of early intervention and safeguarding decisions.

When concerns about a child’s welfare are raised, social services will look at the potential for trauma and risk factors for infants within the home to assess whether they need to intervene.

Here are some reasons newborns are placed in care at birth:

 

  • Previous social services involvement: If the baby’s parents have had older children removed because they were unsafe to live in the home, social services might decide that it’s in the best interests of their unborn child to move into care as soon as they’re born to prevent any harm coming to them.
  • Imprisonment: Although some prisons have mother and baby units, they’re not available in all prisons, and mothers have to be approved to be placed in one. When they’re not, and there is no other suitable caregiver, such as the father or a relative, the newborn baby will move into foster care.
  • Substance misuse: If a mother continues to misuse substances while pregnant, then their child could move into foster care when they’re born.
  • Domestic violence: If there is violence within the home, this puts a newborn baby at immediate risk, resulting in them being taken into care for their safety.
  • Poor mental health: Newborn babies whose parents are suffering from severe mental health conditions might require immediate foster care when they’re born until their parents are well.
  • Illness: If a mother becomes seriously ill, such as during childbirth, and there is no one suitable to care for their newborn baby, the child may need foster care until the mother is well enough to care for their child themselves.
  • Abandonment: Although rare, some mothers might willingly relinquish their child for adoption or leave their baby at the hospital or somewhere else soon after birth. These babies will move into foster care while suitable adoptive parents are found.
  • Parenting capacity: If there are concerns about parenting capacity, the best course of action may be that the mother and/or father move into a foster home with their newborn baby in a parent and child arrangement.

How safeguarding decisions are made

When a safeguarding concern is flagged, either before or after a child is born, a lot goes on behind the scenes to understand the parents’ circumstances and decide on the next steps for the baby’s care.

Local authority (LA) social workers lead investigations and assessments, with the input of other relevant professionals, such as doctors, the police, and childcare providers. If they believe a child is at serious risk, they’ll immediately remove them from their birth family before placing them in an emergency foster home.

What is emergency foster care?

Emergency fostering is a temporary arrangement, lasting between a few days and a few weeks and is the most common type of foster care a baby will first experience. Local authorities (LA) will try to find a suitable home for a baby in their own pool of foster parents, but if they can’t, they’ll refer the child to an independent fostering agency, like us here at FCA.

If you want to provide an emergency foster home for babies, you need to be prepared to welcome them at a moment’s notice, which could be during the day, at night and on weekends. You’ll also need to be comfortable with uncertainty about when a baby will arrive and when they’ll move on, as emergency fostering is primarily there to ensure a child’s safety while the local authority completes their assessments.

What happens next?

Local authority assessments may lead to an interim care order, which means the LA can make plans for a child’s care during court proceedings, such as short-term foster care, kinship care or parent and child fostering.

In other cases, a child may return home following investigations, and the family will be offered additional support.

If court proceedings go ahead, once they conclude, the baby will either return home, live with extended family or be adopted. It’s unlikely that they’ll be fostered long-term, unless they’re part of a sibling group.

Taking babies to family time arrangements

If you become an emergency or short-term foster parent for a baby while court proceedings happen, part of your role will be to take them to family time meetings.

Supervised contact with the birth family can happen as often as two to five times a week when reunification is a possibility.

This means you need to feel comfortable meeting birth parents regularly, often travelling and sometimes at a distance, and remaining non-judgemental, alongside having a schedule flexible enough to facilitate these arrangements.

Understanding birth family circumstances

It can be very easy to blame biological parents for the circumstances that led their newborn baby into care. However, things are rarely ever black and white.

Some parents want to be there for their children, but they just can’t for whatever reason. Others may have had difficult childhoods themselves, which means they don’t know what healthy parenting looks like. And in some cases, they may have had parenting unexpectedly sprung on them and don’t really know what to do.

Although it might be hard, having empathy for birth families when fostering newborns is essential – regardless of what has happened, they’re human and could be feeling guilt, shame, and grief about losing custody of their child.

When you drop your foster child off at birth family contact, you aren’t there to judge; you’re there to provide the care that their child needs while they can’t.

Read our Supporting Babies and Birth Families article to learn more.

Could you foster a child?

If you’d like to learn more about fostering a newborn baby, check out our Understanding the Reality: Fostering Babies article. You’ll discover what a baby actually is in foster care, the most common types of baby fostering, and the practical and emotional realities of choosing this age group.

You can also speak to a member of our knowledgeable team by calling 0800 023 4561 or submit your details via our online form, and they’ll answer any and every question you have about starting your fostering journey.

items.title: Transforming our rental home for children with disabilities: Tracy’s Story
items.snippet: Read Tracy's fostering story and discover how she and her husband adapted their home to provide a loving, accessible family life for two teenagers with complex needs. Learn why she encourages more people to consider fostering children with disabilities. The post Transforming our rental home for children with disabilities: Tracy’s Story appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
Tracy and her husband Andy have been fostering since 2020, switching to FCA in 2024 when they moved back to the UK from Canada.  

The couple cared for two teenagers with complex needs and physical disabilities, even moving house and having it adapted to ensure they can help the girls ‘live life to the fullest’.  

Inspired by the lack of provision for children in foster care living with disabilities, Tracy shared her story to encourage more people to consider opening their home to children with disabilities, and not to be put off by assumptions or perceptions of their needs.   

 

Beginning their fostering journey 

Many of our foster parents start thinking about fostering long before they take the plunge and apply. This was the case for Tracy and Andy, who were fostering six adult children and 11 grandchildren of their own, alongside fostering the two girls in their care.  

Tracy said, “During my time in the NHS, I cared for a little boy with complex needs who used to visit with his foster parent. She told me about the urgent need for foster parents who can support children with disabilities, and I thought, ‘I could do that’ because I’ve always worked in care settings and have a son who has Cerebral Palsy.”  

“From that point on, I had the dream of fostering children with complex needs in the back of my mind. We ended up moving to Canada for a while before moving back to England, where I worked as a nanny.” 

“When the children I was caring for went off to school, I knew that the time was right, and Andy and I started the ball rolling.”  

Transforming their home

When the couple began fostering, their three-bedroom home was suitable. But after being matched with one of their foster daughters, they needed something more accessible.  

Tracy said, “We had to move to a rented house because our foster daughter needed a wet room.” 

“We then worked with an occupational therapist to make sure the house was set up with a ceiling track and hoist equipment too. Our landlord has been great, supporting us to complete the necessary adaptations.” 

“Since then, we’ve also installed a through-floor lift, laid LVT flooring and improved the garden to make it wheelchair-friendly so children can enjoy time outdoors and barbeques.”   

 

Living life to the fullest 

Although caring for two teenagers who required around-the-clock care had challenges, Tracy wants others to know that with careful planning, you can still go on family days out and holidays. She said, “FCA organise group activities that are adapted to different needs.  

“During an event last year, they hoisted one of our foster daughters onto the front of a bicycle, and I was wheeling around with her. It was amazing – she really enjoyed herself.” 

“We also bought a tourer caravan and had all the adaptations done to take the girls with us on trips. If they are part of our family, living with a disability doesn’t mean they should miss out on these experiences.”  

Are you thinking of fostering?

Download the FCA’s complete beginner’s guide to fostering a child. Find out more on how to foster a child and the process involved.

Download Guide

Don’t be put off by assumptions

The couple are encouraging more people to consider fostering children with disabilities, and not to be put off by assumptions or perceptions of their needs. Tracy said, “People look at what we do from the outside and think, ‘I couldn’t do that.’ But Andy and I are living proof that you can.” 

“If you’re interested in applying to foster, I would say give it a go. Make sure you do your research and look into independent fostering agencies rather than just your local authority. It took some time for us to find the right agency for us until we transferred to FCA, but we’re so happy that we did.”  

“Don’t rule out caring for a child with a disability. I promise it’s not as scary as you might think. It’s so rewarding, and it’s a real pleasure to be able to make a huge difference in children’s lives and help them live life to the fullest.”  

 

Could you foster a child with complex needs?  

We asked Tracy to share the qualities she believes are needed for someone to become a foster parent of children with complex needs to show that it’s more accessible than you may have first thought. She said, “You’ve got to be caring, patient, nurturing and adaptable.” 

“Fostering isn’t always easy. We’re all humans, and even the most experienced foster parents have their ups and downs.” 

“You’ve got to be giving of your time and of your heart. You also need to be the kind of person who is willing to ask for help if you need it. At the end of the day, you are welcoming these children into your home, and they’ll become part of your family.  

“You want to do all you can to make the experience as happy and nurturing as possible for them.”  

 

Learn more today 

You don’t need experience to become a foster parent, just a passion for learning and helping others in need.  

If you’d like to learn more about disability fostering, we’d love to hear from you. Call us today on 0800 023 4561 or submit your details via our enquiry form.

Why Cultural Matching Matters in Foster Care
items.snippet: Culture plays a vital role in shaping a child’s identity, sense of belonging, and self-esteem. In foster care, maintaining connections to heritage, traditions, and community can have a positive impact on wellbeing. Learn why cultural matching matters and how foster carers can support children from diverse backgrounds. The post Why Cultural Matching Matters in Foster Care appeared first on Orange Grove Foster Care.
items.content:
We may not realise it if we’ve had the privilege of being consistently exposed to it throughout our lives, but culture plays such an important part in our identity and how we see the world. This is also true for young people in foster care who come from a specific heritage or ethnicity.

These children shouldn’t have to be separated from their culture or people of the same background just because they’re in care. Foster children can sometimes struggle with their sense of identity, so it’s important that they’re matched with foster parents who can help them to explore their traditions and customs.

We’re looking at why cultural matching is so crucial in foster care, and what you can do to support a young person who may not be from the same ethnic or cultural background as yourself. Young people should feel empowered to explore this part of their identity, and part of your role as a foster parent is to help them do just that.

What is culture?

Culture can be defined as the customs, shared beliefs, and values that a group of society use to interpret and understand the world around them. These customs are passed down from generation to generation, and become an important part of our identity. It could include specific types of food, art, music, stories, and language.

These are the building blocks of who we are and what we value as important. By having a shared culture, we can feel a sense of belonging to other people who are like us and share our principles.

Why is it important to consider cultural factors in foster care?

The importance of cultural identity in foster care shouldn’t be underestimated. This can play a massive role in a young person’s self-worth and identity. Being separated from everything they know and love can be incredibly frightening, so we should do everything we can to support them in learning more about their cultural identity.

 

This is crucial for a number of reasons:

  • Creating a sense of belonging – young people who are placed with foster carers who share some aspects of their cultural background are able to better transition into family life, and have a stronger sense of familial identity.
  • Developing an identity – surrounding themselves with people of a similar background or ethnicity can help to create a better sense of identity. A young person can more easily learn about their heritage if they have someone sharing those customs and traditions as they grow older.
  • Learning the navigate the world – knowing more about their cultural identity can often teach young people how to approach the world and any people they meet along the way.
  • Self-worth – if a young person has their religion, diet, specific skin care, hair routines, and language supported by those providing them care, they can foster a sense of cultural pride. This can help to prevent someone from feeling isolated.
  • Resilience to discrimination – if a caregiver is from a similar cultural or ethnic background to the young person in their care, they may have firsthand experience of prejudices that these children may face. This gives you essential tools to pass on to the child in your care of how to deal with similar issues, and you can better understand and support the struggles they may face.
  • Connecting with their heritage – another important aspect is that matching a child with someone of similar culture or ethnicity allows them to maintain a connection with their roots.

 

Matching a child to foster parents of the same ethnicity or culture can often be easier if this is a long-term fostering placement. However, we will do everything we can to match a child with a family from a similar background if this is possible in short term placements.

Child-led decisions

While cultural matching is an important thing to bear in mind, it’s also crucial to consider what the foster child would want in terms of matching. If they don’t want to be placed with foster parents who share certain characteristics, such as ethnicity or religion, then we listen to their preferences wherever possible.

However, if a foster child shows an interest in connecting with their heritage as part of their identity, we ensure that they have the opportunity to do so. That could be by reading books from authors of a similar background, meeting similar people in a social setting, or supporting them to do research into the history of their culture.

Fostering siblings

Sadly, a lot of sibling groups end up in care. Opening your heart and home to a sibling group can help them to foster their sense of cultural identity together. They have a shared history, and if they’re able to stay together in foster care then they’re better able to navigate their sense of identity and where they came from.

If fostering siblings is something that you would be interested in, our friendly team of advisors can talk you through the fostering process in more detail on 0800 369 8513.

Supporting cultural identity

While we try our best to make sure that we match children with foster parents of a similar ethnicity or background, sometimes this won’t be possible. There is a national shortage of foster parents across the UK, with a 10% decline since 2021. This means it’s not always possible for children to be matched with a family from a similar background, whether that’s for a short-term or long-term placement.

In this case, it’s important that you’re able to support your foster child’s cultural identity in whichever way you can.

This can be done in a variety of ways:

  • Training – we offer a range of training courses to our foster parents to help them support their foster child if they’re from a different culture or ethnicity to themselves.
  • Specialist hair salons – some children may need to be taken to a specialist hair salon to accommodate their needs. For example, finding a salon that knows how to work with and care for black hair.
  • Research – you should try your best to learn more about your foster child’s life history, cultural background, and beliefs. By improving your understanding of their heritage, you’ll be better able to support the needs of your foster child.
  • Religion – if a particular religion is important to your foster child’s identity, you can support them by including this worship in their day-to-day lives. Respect any dietary requirements if this is part of their faith, such as abstaining from certain food items.
  • Try new foods – if there’s a specific type of cuisine that is inherent in your foster child’s culture, try new recipes with them. Let them choose a recipe they would like to make, and cook it together.
  • Language – if your foster child speaks a different language to you, it will be worth learning a few key phrases that you can speak with them so they feel more at home.
  • Ask your foster child – the best way to support your foster child and their needs is to speak to them and ask how they would like your help to connect with their heritage. They might give you some ideas that you hadn’t thought of, and they may really appreciate your thoughtfulness.
  • Fashion – if there are specific clothes that your foster child would like to wear because it’s important to them as part of their identity, try to accommodate their needs where you can.

Could you open your home to a foster child in need?

Are you passionate about your heritage and want to help young people from the same culture in foster care? Opening up your home and heart to those in need could have a massively positive impact on their future.

If you’re curious to know more about foster care requirements and how you could make a difference in a child’s life, simply fill out an enquiry form on our website or give us a ring on 0800 369 8513 to speak to one of our friendly advisors. They can talk to you about the fostering process and foster care requirements in more detail.

items.title: School Leavers Drive to The Finish Line!
items.snippet: TACT's Yorkshire and North East teams took a group of school leavers on an unforgettable driving experience. The post School Leavers Drive to The Finish Line! appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
School Leavers Drive to The Finish Line!

Our TACT Yorkshire and North East teams took a group of school leavers on a driving experience that was not only exhilarating – it provided an opportunity for young people to socialise and make new friends.

To celebrate the hard work and dedication our young people have shown in their exams and finishing school, we organised our first school leavers event in July which took place at  Elvington Airfield in York. A Youth Driving Experience was the activity – and it did not disappoint!

Each young person got to choose a super sports car to drive with an instructor. They got to drive three miles round a track in their chosen car – out of a Ferrari, Lamborghini, Porsche or Audi.

After their drive they hopped into a F1 Atom where a driver took them on a high-speed drive. They all did amazing, listening and following instructions to keep safe whilst enjoying the experience.

 They all absolutely loved the day; below are some quotes directly from our young people:

“It was different, exciting and fun. It’s a fun and unexpected activity in which I enjoyed driving the car which was the best bit”

“You get to meet with other people your own age which can benefit you and it’s good to feel like you’re not alone”

“I really enjoyed everything, the instructor advised me to slow down but I wanted to go faster”

“I like the teen only events because I get to meet others and do activities I’ve not done before. I usually struggle and don’t like talking to new people”

Activity days such as this are so important for our young people, not only as a celebration and reflection of hard work and achievement, but also as an opportunity to come together and share experiences and make new friends. A big thank you to our Yorkshire and North East teams for organising such a valuable day of wellbeing!

items.title: Taking a Foster Child on Holiday: Things You Need to Know
items.snippet: Planning a holiday with your foster child can be an exciting opportunity to create lasting memories together. Before you travel, it’s important to understand the permissions required and how to support your child’s needs. Discover practical tips for a smooth, enjoyable, and stress-free family holiday. The post Taking a Foster Child on Holiday: Things You Need to Know appeared first on Fosterplus.
items.content:
If it’s right for your family and your foster child, going on holiday for the first time is so exciting. You get to see their faces light up as they experience new things, no matter if that’s a staycation in the UK with younger children or somewhere more exotic if you’re fostering teenagers.

But before you start to make concrete plans for your next family holiday, there are a few things that you’ll need to bear in mind when it comes to taking your foster children with you.

From permissions to managing expectations and anxieties, we’re going to take a closer look at everything you need to know about taking your foster children on holiday.

Can you take your foster child on holiday abroad?

Yes, you can take your foster child abroad – if it’s suitable for them – but you’ll need to get permission from either their birth parents or the local authority first. Check the legal order for your foster child to see which permissions you need to secure before you can take them on holiday. You’ll need to make sure that you’ve got proper documentation, such as a passport for your foster child, too.

If your foster child has never been on a holiday with your family before, it’s best to take your foster child on a staycation in the UK first. This can get them used to going on holidays and show them this is an exciting time for all the family, especially if they’re in long-term foster care.

Travelling abroad with your foster child for the first time is exciting, and you can show them new experiences, such as going on a plane, seeing the sea in warmer climates, or trying food local to the country you’re visiting. Remember to stick to the same mealtime and bedtime routines, though, so your foster child still has a sense of stability.

 

Holidaying abroad checklist

  • Passports – make sure you’ve got these to hand. If your foster child doesn’t have a passport, you’ll need to talk to your social worker. They can get a passport for your foster child if they have permission from whoever has parental responsibility. Make sure to allow plenty of time for this to arrive before you book anything.
  • Letter of permission – chances are you won’t have to use it, but it’s a good idea to have a letter of permission from the local authority to hand to prove that you’re the children’s foster parents.
  • Medicine – if your foster child needs regular medication such as asthma inhalers or insulin, make sure you’ve got plenty to last you the length of your stay abroad. You may also need to have a letter from your foster child’s doctor if their medicine contains a controlled drug. Having a first aid kit to hand could also come in useful.
  • Comfort toys – let your foster child choose a soft toy or fidget toy to bring with them for the duration of your holiday. This will give them something comforting from back home to soothe them if there are any wobbly moments.
  • Sleeping arrangements – these will need to be carefully considered when you’re booking your holiday. Some children may still need a separate room, while others may be allowed to share. Talk to your supervising social worker to see what they would advise for your circumstances, as they’ll also need to fill out a risk assessment form.

Holidaying in the UK

There are plenty of places here in the UK that make ideal locations for a staycation, and you won’t be too far away from home if you need to change your plans at the last minute and cut your break short. Plus, this is an excellent way to introduce your foster children to holidays if this is all new to them.

Holidays can spark big emotions for some children, as it means being removed from the safety and security of home. We’ve got some top tips below to help you prepare for time away, but it’s important to let your foster child know at each step where you’re going and how long for.

They may need reassurance that they’ll be with you at all times, they won’t be going anywhere on their own, and that they’ll be coming back home with you afterwards. Your supervising social worker can advise you of what other things you’ll need to bear in mind, too.

Staycation top tips

  • Permissions – even though you’re not planning on going abroad, you’ll still need to make sure that you’ve got all the right permissions in place before you go on your holiday.
  • Start small – before you book those weeklong holidays, it’ll be worth taking your foster child on smaller weekend breaks so that they can get used to going away with you. You can slowly work up to longer breaks or even go abroad.
  • Maintaining routines – holidays can cause big emotions to come into play if your foster child feels unsettled. The best way to avoid complicated feelings is to stick to your routines as much as possible, in terms of bedtimes and mealtimes.
  • Plan lots of downtime – although holidays are an exciting time, being out of their usual routine, among busy crowds, or in unfamiliar surroundings can take a toll on your foster child’s emotions. Think about what you’re going to do if or when they become dysregulated so that you can help them work through their feelings. Planning lots of downtime into your schedule can also help them when they start to feel overwhelmed.

Preparation is key

Going away from their place of safety, such as your home, can trigger complex feelings for your foster child. Stability and routine are so important for children in care, as this can give them the sense of security they need to overcome past trauma.

Here are some of our top tips to help you prepare your foster children for any holidays you want to take them on in the future:

  • Get them involved in the planning process – one of the best ways to manage any anxieties about holidays is to ask your foster child what they would like to do or where they would like to go.
  • Take them to see the airport – a couple of times before you’re due to fly out, if you’re going abroad, take your foster children to the airport to watch the planes take off and land. This could help alleviate any nervous feelings about flying.
  • Show them videos of where you’re going – letting your foster children watch videos of the hotel, cottage, beaches, and the dining room with food can help to ease any worries they may have.
  • Snacks – let your foster children choose snacks to take with them on the journey.
  • Toys and activities – allow your foster children to select a soft toy, colouring or puzzle book, and fidget toys to bring with them for the journey.
  • Choosing their own cases – give your foster children the option to choose their own cases for the trip, within reason. This can show them that holidays are an exciting thing for them, too.
  • Acknowledge their feelings – before you leave for the holiday, make sure you acknowledge any worries or concerns your foster children may have. Remind them that they won’t be on their own. Anywhere you go, you’ll be going together, and they’ll be coming back home with you. This is an exciting time, and they’re bound to have fun, no matter where you go together.

If your foster child finds the whole experience too overwhelming, don’t be afraid to cut your break short. Their welfare is the most important thing, and you wouldn’t want to distress them further if they’d rather be at home with all their comforts.

Chances are that if you give them plenty of time to get used to the idea of going on holiday and allow them to mentally prepare for the experience, you won’t need to come home early. But it’s worth considering cutting things short if your foster child becomes dysregulated often while you’re away. You can work up to longer breaks away over time.

Curious about fostering?

Fostering is one of the most rewarding things you can choose to do. If you want to learn more about the different types of fostering and whether this is the right step for you and your family, we’re here to help.

Simply fill out an enquiry form on our website or give us a ring on 0800 369 8512 to speak to one of our friendly advisors who can talk you through the fostering process in more detail.

Taking that initial first step on your fostering journey could be the best decision you’ve ever made, allowing you to make a difference in a young person’s life.

items.title: TACT’s Aspirational Fund Helps Budding Pilot To Fly
items.snippet: TACT's Aspirational Fund has enabled a young person to take his first steps towards becoming a pilot in the South West. The post TACT’s Aspirational Fund Helps Budding Pilot To Fly appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT’s Aspirational Fund Helps Budding Pilot To Fly

A special fund used to provide TACT’s young people with potentially life-changing opportunities has enabled a 12 year old young person to get one step closer to their dream of becoming a pilot.

TACT’s Aspirational Fund has already been used to fuel new hobbies, so when one of our young people expressed an interest in planes, we swooped in to help him realise his dream.

‘A’s interest started around 3 years ago when he came across a video about planes and was immediately fascinated. He began taking flying lessons, but these turned out to be expensive. His social worker and TACT South West Area Manager Sara Gullick recognised his interest continuing to grow, so they offered to pay for one of the lessons using the Aspiration Fund.

A said: “Of course, I didn’t fly the plane by myself, I had an instructor with me who would do the hard bits like taking off and landing, but the rest was up to me.” He also described how the planes he’s flown weren’t commercial planes as they were “small with one engine”. He said that he would like to “become a pilot where I fly big planes!”.

It’s incredible that the Aspiration Fund has been able to help a young person pursue their dreams and we hope that one day A will achieve his goal of becoming a pilot.

items.title: Therapeutic Support ‘Clinics’ For West Midlands Foster Carers
items.snippet: TACT have commissioned specialist therapeutic support 'clinics' for their foster carers in the West Midlands. The post Therapeutic Support ‘Clinics’ For West Midlands Foster Carers appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Therapeutic Support ‘Clinics’ For West Midlands Foster Carers

TACT’s dedicated Health Service have commissioned specialist therapeutic support ‘clinics’ for their foster carers in the West Midlands, via their Health Framework Contract model – with a view to possibly extending the support to other regions.

The consultation clinics, led by Vicki McKeown from VLM Therapy, were commissioned to provide TACT’s foster carers with a space where they could bring the children and young people they provide care for, to think through any difficulties or worries they might be experiencing with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma-informed practice.

The aim of the clinics is to help carers feel more confident and less alone when faced with challenging or confusing behaviour, while strengthening the carer and child relationship. Understanding a child’s attachment pattern gives carers a lens for seeing behaviour as communication which changes how they respond, and changes what the child experiences as safe.

Before the clinics, Vicki is provided with information in advance about a child’s history, their current relationship dynamics with their birth family and carers, and their day-to-day behaviours and presenting difficulties. Together with the carer, they then use the clinic to understand these behaviours from an attachment and trauma perspective, drawing on theory while looking at how it applies in real life to that particular child. They talk through any specific difficulties or triggering situations and explore strategies and tools that the carer can use to respond. The aim is to upskill the carer so they leave with a deeper understanding and practical ways of supporting the child going forward.

Mechelle Holley, TACT’s Health Commissioning & Performance Manager, said: “Setting up the clinics has been a real collaborative piece of work. I really enjoyed supporting the team to reflect on the different options available through the framework, and facilitating access to providers who I feel confident can take the vision and work with the team to create a finished service that truly focuses on outcomes for children and young people.

“I’ve really seen the benefits of creating space for honest conversations about what children and young people need. The framework has helped bring together a committed area team and a provider who share similar values, enabling them to build a positive working relationship and shape a model of support that feels both responsive and sustainable. It’s been great to see that partnership develop with a genuine focus on ensuring children and young people can access the right support at the right time and have their needs understood and met. I’m really excited to see how things continue to develop as those relationships strengthen and the team and Vicki continue to learn from one another and grow the offer together.”

“Setting up the clinics has been a real collaborative piece of work. I really enjoyed supporting the team to reflect on the different options available through the framework, and facilitating access to providers who I feel confident can take the vision and work with the team to create a finished service that truly focuses on outcomes for children and young people.”

Mechelle Holley, TACT’s Health Commissioning & Performance Manager

From a commissioning perspective, using the Health Framework Contract to deliver these interventions enables TACT to secure a high-quality, cost-effective service that supports positive outcomes for children and young people and strengthens placement stability.

The feedback from carers so far has been positive, illustrating just how useful the clinics have been. One carer shared: “I gained clear guidance on building a secure attachment, along with many additional tips and insights I didn’t even realise I needed. I left feeling far more confident and equipped in my role as a foster carer.”

Clinics are currently running bi-monthly across the West Midlands, and other areas within TACT are also exploring whether this is something that would work for their region.

The post Therapeutic Support ‘Clinics’ For West Midlands Foster Carers appeared first on TACT.

items.title: From Bearded Biker to Foster Dad: Tim’s Fostering Story
items.snippet: From biker and former doorman to devoted foster dad, Tim Jarvis is proving there’s no such thing as a “typical” foster parent. Discover how a journey that began with a 10-year plan turned into 12 years of changing young lives, challenging stereotypes, and creating a forever family. The post From Bearded Biker to Foster Dad: Tim’s Fostering Story appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
Tim isn’t your stereotypical foster dad – he’s a biker, former doorman, and has a well-established beard.

He and his wife Claire have been fostering with FCA West Midlands for more than 12 years, and in that time, their journey has taken them in many unexpected directions.

From why they chose fostering and how it all began to challenging outdated stereotypes and encouraging others not to write themselves off as foster parents, Tim shares his fostering story and words of wisdom for those thinking about joining him in transforming young lives.

“Having kids was impossible”

In 2008, Tim fought testicular cancer and the treatment he received meant that he was unlikely to be able to conceive a biological child. Not only that, but he and Claire had reservations about bringing a child into this turbulent world, so they decided fostering was their route into experiencing parenthood.

Tim said, “We didn’t have any children of our own before fostering. My first child was a foster child, and she was a bridesmaid at our wedding and even came on our ‘family moon’.”

12 years on, the couple have a biological son, have adopted one of the children they fostered, and are fostering a teenager, even converting their garage a few years ago to make more space for children and teenagers who need a loving home.

“I’m not your average foster parent”

The average age of a foster parent is 54, and of these, around 80% are female. Many are empty nesters and often transition from professions closely linked to fostering, such as social care, nursing, and teaching.

Tim is challenging these norms, he said, “I’m not your average foster parent because I have a beard, love motorbikes and used to be a doorman; people don’t expect you to go from that to fostering.”

“I suppose when someone thinks about a foster parent, they probably imagine a sweet older lady with grown-up children who lives round the corner, but that’s not our experience of fostering, it’s one of the most diverse groups of people you can imagine.”

“I don’t look like a typical foster parent, and when our most recent foster daughter arrived, she was definitely a bit intimidated by me. She even told me that. But now we know each other, and she’s just part of the family.”

“Don’t write yourself off as a foster parent just because you don’t fit the conventional demographic. You’ll have something to bring to these children, regardless of your background, age, or gender.”

Are you thinking of fostering?

Download the FCA’s complete beginner’s guide to fostering a child. Find out more on how to foster a child and the process involved.

Download Guide

 “I don’t care how old the kid is; I just want to change a life.”

Tim and Claire don’t let anything faze them. Their fostering journey has taken many twists and turns, with one of the biggest being that they were down to foster children over 12 but ended up fostering a baby, whom they later adopted.

Tim explained, “We were always down to foster kids aged over 12 because they’re more independent – they can get themselves dressed, feed themselves, and take the bus to school.”

“That all changed one afternoon, when we got a phone call about a baby. They were like, ‘We’ve got a baby… It’s an emergency. Can you have her?’ And I immediately said, ‘Yes, of course we can’ because how can you say no?”

“I said I wanted a teen that I wouldn’t have to feed and parent like a baby. And look what happened. We ended up adopting her. At the end of the day, I don’t care how old the kid is; I just want to change a life.”

“Just do it. What have you got to lose?”

Every year, around 39,000 children enter care, but there is a shortage of more than 6,000 foster parents to care for them.

Tim is urging those who have room in their heart and home to come forward and help bridge this gap, he said: “Just do it. What have you got to lose?”

“Yes, it can be challenging, and you’ve got to be open-minded, but it is the most rewarding thing I’ve ever done. I love it, and if I get the chance to do it again in a second life, I will.”

“It might be for you, it might not. But unless you do it, you won’t know.”

Inspired by Tim’s Story? Get in touch

If, like Tim and Claire, you’d like to make a difference to vulnerable children and young people by becoming a foster parent, call us on 0800 023 4561 or submit your details via our enquiry form.

Our experienced team will take you through the initial requirements and answer any burning questions you may have.

You can also find out more about the ins and outs of fostering with FCA by checking out our blogs and reading more of our fostering stories, right here online.

items.title: Why Foster Carers Are Needed
items.snippet: Foster carers provide far more than a place to stay, they offer a safe and nurturing home where children can feel secure, rebuild trust and begin to thrive. The post Why Foster Carers Are Needed appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
Every child deserves to feel safe, valued and cared for. Yet across the UK, more than 81,000 children are currently in care, and over 7,200 additional fostering households are needed to meet growing demand.

Behind these statistics are children facing challenging circumstances who need stability, support and someone who will listen to them. Foster carers provide far more than a place to stay, they offer a safe and nurturing home where children can feel secure, rebuild trust and begin to thrive. Through kindness, encouragement and consistent care, foster carers help children develop confidence and look towards the future with hope.

As the demand for foster carers continues to grow, more people have the opportunity to make a lasting and meaningful difference in a child’s life, providing the support and security they need when it matters most.

The growing need for foster carers

More children are entering care each year, increasing the need for foster carers across the UK. When there are not enough local fostering households, children may have to move away from their siblings, schools, friends and support networks, creating even more disruption during an already difficult time.

Remaining close to familiar places and people can make a significant difference to a child’s emotional wellbeing. Local foster carers help children maintain routines, continue their education and stay connected to the communities that matter most to them.

Children come into care for many different reasons, through no fault of their own. While every child’s experience is unique, they all deserve a nurturing environment where they can begin to recover from difficult experiences and thrive.

Foster care is about more than providing a home

Fostering is about creating a stable and caring environment where every day routines such as sharing meals, getting ready for school, celebrating achievements and taking time to listen help children develop and build confidence.

With the right support, children are better able to engage with education, explore new interests and develop important life skills. Whether it is cheering from the sidelines at a football match, helping with homework or celebrating a school achievement, foster carers play an important role in encouraging children to reach their potential.

As young people grow older, foster carers also help prepare them for adulthood by teaching practical skills such as cooking, budgeting and planning for employment or further education. These experiences give young people greater independence as they move towards adult life.

The difference foster carers make

Often, it is the smallest moments that have the greatest impact. A calm conversation after a difficult day, a familiar morning routine, a packed lunch prepared with care or simply knowing that someone is there to listen can help a child feel safe and valued.

These everyday acts of kindness create the consistency many children have been missing. Over time, they help strengthen self-esteem and provide the foundation children need to achieve their potential.

As Swiis foster carer Bianca explains:

“We have witnessed growth in every way with both children, and their happiness knows no bounds. We are confident in our journey knowing that the children trust us.”

Read Bianca and Jermell’s Fostering Story

The voices of children and young people in our care offer an equally powerful reminder of the impact a loving foster family can have. In a personal letter about their experience in foster care, one young person wrote:

“[My foster carers] are the reason I am the person I am today… I feel like I will actually have someone to help me through any hard times I have, someone I can actually talk to about things. I am no longer afraid of growing up, because I know that I am surrounded by amazing people who will support me and be there for me through thick and thin.”

Have a read of the full ‘Why I want to stay with my foster carers’ letter

Why become a foster carer?

People choose to become foster carers for many reasons, but they all share a desire to make a meaningful difference to a child’s life.

Fostering can be both rewarding and challenging, requiring patience, resilience and understanding. While every fostering journey is different, Swiis foster carers are never expected to manage alone.

Many describe fostering as life changing, not only for the children they care for but for themselves as well. Watching a child overcome challenges and achieve milestones can be one of the most rewarding experiences a person can have.

How Swiis supports foster carers

At Swiis, we support foster carers throughout every stage of their fostering journey. From your first enquiry through to your care arrangement, you will be part of an experienced and supportive network.

Our foster carers receive comprehensive training, ongoing guidance and access to dedicated professionals such as health and education advisors, to help them provide the best possible care for the children they look after.

We are committed to helping children achieve positive outcomes while ensuring every foster carer feels respected and supported in their role.

Take the next step

By becoming a foster carer, you could provide the stability, encouragement and care that helps a young person build a brighter future. With more foster carers needed across the UK than ever before, your decision could make a lasting difference to a child’s life.

If you would like to find out more about becoming a foster carer with Swiis, our friendly recruitment team is here to help. They will be happy to guide you through the fostering process, explain the support, training and allowances available, and answer any questions you may have.

The post Why Foster Carers Are Needed appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.

items.title: FCA Yorks and Lincs Staff and Carer Forum at Aston Hall
items.snippet: Staff and foster parents from across Yorkshire and Lincolnshire gathered at Aston Hall for a successful Staff and Carer Forum, featuring insightful presentations on supporting children in care, including a powerful contribution from care-experienced Social Work Student Nakita. The post FCA Yorks and Lincs Staff and Carer Forum at Aston Hall appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
Staff and foster parents from across Yorks and Lincs recently came together for a successful and engaging Staff and Carer Forum, held in the beautiful surroundings of Aston Hall.

The day began with a warm welcome as attendees enjoyed a cuppa and a selection of morning pastries, providing a great opportunity for colleagues and carers from across the region to connect, catch up, and share experiences before the forum commenced.

The event was opened by our Deputy to the Registered Manager Jo Charity who welcomed everyone to the forum and introduced several new members of staff. Attendees were also updated on the latest developments across the region, celebrating achievements and sharing important information about ongoing initiatives and plans.

One of the highlights of the day was an insightful presentation delivered by Jane Batley on the topic of shame and how it can present in the children and young people we support. Jane’s thought-provoking session encouraged attendees to reflect on how feelings of shame can influence behaviour, relationships, and emotional wellbeing, while also providing practical strategies to help children feel understood, valued, and supported.

The forum was further enriched by a powerful contribution from our Peterborough team. Nakita, a care-experienced Social Work Student, spoke eloquently about her journey and experiences, offering valuable reflections that resonated strongly with attendees.

Nakita shared her personal journey and reflections with the group. Her honest and inspiring account offered a unique perspective on the care experience and highlighted the lasting impact that positive, supportive relationships can have on young people. Nakita ’s presentation was both moving and thought-provoking, leaving a lasting impression on everyone in attendance.

Throughout the day, staff and foster parents were encouraged to share ideas, ask questions, and contribute to discussions, reinforcing the collaborative approach that is at the heart of our service. The forum provided a valuable opportunity to learn from one another, celebrate successes, and strengthen the relationships that help us achieve the best outcomes for children and young people.

One foster parent made the following comment, “An incredibly insightful and eye-opening presentation. It was a deeply moving session that provided both professional insights and personal food for thought. The interview with Nakita was a powerful reminder of the failures and successes of a child in the care system.  Her journey at 25 stands as a testament to her personal resilience but her reflection serves as an urgent call to action for the social care sector to cultivate empathy and treat every child as inherently worthy of success. The forum delivered what traditional training often misses. The raw unfiltered truth of lived experience. There is no substitute for hearing  directly from people who have lived through the system”

A huge thank you goes to everyone who attended and contributed to making the day such a success. We look forward to seeing everyone again at our next regional forum.

If you’d like to find out more about fostering with FCA, please get in touch with our friendly team today.

items.title: Putting Children Before Profit Starts with More Foster Carers
items.snippet: Residential homes for children are costing local authorities tens of thousands of pounds per week, and should be a wake-up call. But the issue runs deeper than money. The post Putting Children Before Profit Starts with More Foster Carers appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Putting Children Before Profit Starts with More Foster Carers

A recent Times article highlighted the shocking reality that residential placements for children are costing local authorities tens of thousands of pounds per week. This should be a wake-up call for everyone involved in children’s social care. The costs are staggering – but the real issue goes deeper than money.  

Too many children are living in residential care because there simply aren’t enough foster families available to meet their needs. If we want to reduce the opportunity for profiteering in the care system, we need to increase the number of loving, well-supported foster homes children can move into. 

Of course, residential care has an important role to play in the sector. For some children, it is absolutely the right setting and can provide specialist support that cannot be delivered elsewhere. But for many children, a loving family home could offer the stability, relationships and sense of belonging they need to thrive. The challenge is that there simply aren’t enough foster carers willing and able to support them. 

That’s why TACT has launched Step Forward – a specialist fostering programme designed to help children move from residential care into stable family environments.

Step Forward Fostering provides enhanced support, therapeutic training, a strong network around carers and children, and a model specifically designed to support children who are currently living in a residential setting. 

For people with experience working with children, young people or in caring roles, Step Forward can also offer a meaningful alternative to a traditional career path. It provides the opportunity to use professional skills and life experience in a deeply personal, practical way, while receiving specialist training, wraparound support and a financial package that makes fostering a realistic option for people who may not previously have thought it was possible. 

As a not-for-profit fostering charity, we believe public money should be invested in children and families, not extracted as profit. Our focus is simple: better outcomes for children, stronger partnerships with local authorities, and greater social value for communities. If we want to reduce reliance on expensive residential placements, improve outcomes for children and create a more sustainable care system, we need more people to consider fostering. 

We need experienced, compassionate individuals who can help a child take the next step from residential care into family life. We need more people to Step Forward and help transform a child’s future.
