items.title: Ideas for Couples Who Can’t Have Children
items.snippet: There are a few of ways to start a new family. Here are some options you can consider when you can’t have children. The post Ideas for Couples Who Can’t Have Children appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
If you’re facing challenges starting your family, we know how heartbreaking and devastating it can feel.

You may be struggling to come to terms with being unable to conceive through traditional means, but when you’re ready, there are many alternative routes to parenthood that couples can explore.

Although it might not be the road you thought you’d go down, dreams of building a beautiful and loving family can still become a reality. From fertility treatments to fostering, join us as we explore alternative ways to start a family.

Accepting you can’t have a baby conventionally

Before you start researching different ways to have a baby, you may need to take some time to process the idea of not having children or another child in the traditional way.

How you do this looks different for every person, but giving yourself time to contemplate can help you recognise which route into starting or growing your family would be most suitable for you.

You may find it beneficial to talk to a therapist or counsellor who can help you work through your feelings and find a way to accept your circumstances before exploring your choices.

Alternative ways to have a family

Whether you’re a couple, single or LGBTQIA+, there are many options to consider. Each one will have its own pros and cons, so deciding the route that is right for you will be down to your personal experiences and preferences.

1. Fertility Treatments

If you haven’t already, speak to a fertility specialist. They will be able to assess whether you or your partner has any underlying health conditions that could make conceiving more challenging. The fertility doctor may then recommend surgery, medication, or assisted conception to help you and your partner have better chances of conceiving.

Surgery

  • In some cases, your doctor may advise surgery, such as:
  • If you’re a woman and have a condition like endometriosis, fibroids, or blocked fallopian tubes.
  • If you’re a man and have a condition such as a blocked epididymis, which can affect ejaculation.
  • If you’re a man, they may extract sperm if you have had an unsuccessful vasectomy reversal or have a condition that prevents sperm from being released.

Please bear in mind that although surgery might be a good option for you, it isn’t a guarantee that you’ll be able to conceive.

Like with any surgery, there will be risks involved, but your doctor should talk these through with you. Don’t be afraid to ask questions about recovery times, success rates, and pain management so you can make an informed decision.

Fertility Medication

Another option doctors might consider is prescribing fertility medications. Here are some scenarios where this might happen:

  • If you don’t ovulate every month or at all, medications such as Clomifene, Tamoxifen, or Gonadotrophins might be prescribed to encourage ovulation.
  • If you have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a doctor may prescribe Metformin to reduce insulin levels that can impact ovulation.
  • If you’re a man with low sperm mobility, Gonadotrophins might be prescribed to stimulate the production of sperm.

Although fertility medications could help you conceive a child, you may experience side effects when taking them, and they aren’t always suitable for everyone. If a medical professional does suggest this kind of treatment, take time to reflect on whether it is the right pathway for you before agreeing to go ahead.

Assisted Conception

If you’re a heterosexual couple, a same-sex couple, or a single woman, assisted conception could help you conceive.

Assisted conception procedures include:

  • In vitro fertilisation (IVF): This procedure involves harvesting an egg and sperm from each partner or donor before combining them in a laboratory. If the combination is successful, embryos are implanted into the woman’s uterus.
  • Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI): This procedure is similar to IVF, but instead of allowing the sperm to fertilise the egg on its own, the sperm is injected directly into the egg.
  • Intrauterine insemination (IUI): sperm from a male partner or donor is inserted directly into the uterus when the woman is ovulating.

The NHS offer some assisted conception procedures, depending on whether you meet the eligibility criteria in your local area. Criteria can include age, amount of time you’ve been trying to conceive, and having no children. If you don’t meet the criteria, you may be able to receive treatment through a private clinic.

Like fertility medication and surgery, assisted conception comes with risks that your doctor should discuss with you before you go down this route.

2. Fostering

For many people who are unable to have children biologically, fostering gives them the chance to experience family life while making a life-changing difference to a child or young person.

As a foster parent, you’ll care for children who are unable to live with their birth families, helping them move forward by offering them stability, guidance, and support. It’s more flexible than adoption and the only family-building option where you’ll receive an allowance to care for a child.

There are many types of fostering, and signing up with an independent fostering agency like ours will provide you with the most options. Whether you give children and young people a temporary home in an emergency or a permanent home as a long-term foster parent, fostering will change your life and theirs.

FCA foster mum Tiffany started her fostering journey in 2024 after she and her partner struggled to conceive for a couple of years, and they have never looked back.

Tiffany said, “Every small moment makes fostering special. The girls moved in with us mid-summer holidays, so we took them to the beach, and we found out that it was their first time. Seeing their faces light up – in the sand, building sandcastles, just being themselves and having so much fun – was incredible.” Read Tiffany’s fostering story.

We’ll explore fostering in more detail later in this guide.

3. Surrogacy

If you’re a same-sex couple, if pregnancy poses health risks, or if it isn’t possible to carry a pregnancy to term, surrogacy could be an option for you. Surrogacy means selecting a woman who is both healthy and willing to carry your baby and give birth to them.

Many couples choose someone they know, while others work with a fertility clinic to select a suitable surrogate they’ve never met before. An embryo is either donated or created by the parents before being implanted into the surrogate’s uterus.

Although surrogacy is legal in the UK, you can only pay for a surrogate’s expenses. When they give birth to your child, they will have parental responsibility until you have applied for a parental order or adopted the child.

4. Adoption

Adoption is where you become the legal parents of a non-biological child, and the rights of the birth parents are removed and transferred to you. It’s a wonderful way to build your family and give a vulnerable child a loving, new home.

With adoption, there are children and young people of all ages who need new homes and families, from newborn babies up to older teenagers.

To adopt, you need to apply through an adoption agency, and there is a two-stage process that takes about six months to complete. If approved, the agency will try to match you with a child, followed by a few weeks of planned introductions. If everything is successful, the child will move into your home.

This table shows the differences between the options we’ve provided, making it much clearer to compare them and decide which route may be best for you and your family.

Option Time to Start Cost Flexibility Support
IVF Long High Low Medical
Adoption Long Medium Low Agency
Fostering Faster Paid High Ongoing

Why fostering could be right for you

Of all the family-building options available, fostering is unique because not only will you get to experience the rewards of parenthood, but you’ll also help the most vulnerable children and young people in society by providing them a safe, stable, and loving home.

There’s currently a shortage of around 6,000 foster parents in the UK, which means children who’ve already been through the unimaginable face being separated from their siblings, living far from the communities they know, or living in residential care.

There are a lot of misconceptions about fostering, which can put people off choosing it as a way to build their family. So let’s look at the facts so you can make an informed decision about whether becoming a foster parent is a viable route into parenthood for you.

What are the requirements to foster a child?

One reason many people choose fostering is its accessibility. You can apply whether you’re single, married, in a same-sex relationship, already have children or have experienced fertility challenges yourself.

All you need to do is meet the following initial criteria:

  • You must be over 21
  • You must have a spare bedroom
  • You must have the legal right to live and work in the UK
  • A passion for changing the lives of vulnerable children and young people

Do you need previous parenting experience?

No, you don’t need previous parenting experience to become a foster parent. At FCA, you’ll receive 24/7 support from fostering experts, and when you join us, you’ll enrol in our professional training programme where you’ll learn everything you need to know about looking after a foster child.

You’ll also benefit from the following:

  • Generous fostering allowances: To cover the expenses of having a child in your care and reward you for your hard work and dedication.
  • Bonuses: Every year, you’ll receive a summer and winter bonus.
  • Rewards: You’ll have easy access to discounts to cut the costs of days out, meals, and groceries.
  • Our Stars Scheme: This exclusive scheme acknowledges, rewards and appreciates all our foster parents.
  • Activities & Events: From the Big Sing Off  to coffee and cake, we organise activities and events so you can make friends, have fun and enjoy life as a foster parent.

 

Is fostering hard?

Like parenting, fostering can be challenging at times, but the difference is the support you receive. While some parents have a village to lean on, that’s not the case for every family, especially if relatives live far away or have other commitments.

But when you foster with FCA, support comes as standard from the very moment you enquire. Fostering is not something you do alone; it’s a community effort, and we’ll make sure you have the support you need whenever you need it.

We call it Team Parenting, and it includes specialist input from fostering professionals, such as social workers, education leads, a participation team, and therapists. You’ll also have lots of opportunities to get to know other foster parents in your local area.

How long will the application process take?

It takes around four to six months to become a foster parent and involves six steps:

  • Enquiry: Get in touch with our team by phone or online. We’ll answer your questions and explain what fostering involves.
  • Home Visit: A fostering advisor will visit your home (or arrange a virtual call) to get to know you and talk through your situation.
  • Application: If you’re ready, you’ll complete an application form, and we’ll begin background checks and references.
  • Fostering Assessment: A social worker will work closely with you to understand your experience, lifestyle, and support network.
  • Training: You’ll complete expert-led training designed to prepare you for real-life fostering situations – so you feel confident from day one.
  • Panel & Approval: An independent panel will review your application before a final decision is made.

Can I try fostering before committing?

Fostering isn’t something you can really try before committing. But you can learn more about what it’s really like by reading our foster parent stories.

You might also consider providing respite foster care before opening your home to a child for a longer term. Respite care is typically arranged in advance, and you’ll look after a child for a few nights up to two weeks while their full-time foster parents take a break.

You’ll still need to complete the same application and assessment process, but it means that if you decide that you’d like to offer long-term foster care, you’ll already be approved.

Can you adopt a foster child?

The goal is always to reunite foster children with their birth parents if and when it’s considered safe to do so; however, that doesn’t always happen. If you foster a child long-term, you may form a beautiful bond to the point where adoption makes sense.

Although it is not always straightforward, adopting a foster child is possible. You’d need to speak with your foster agency and social workers about your intentions, as ultimately, it will come down to what’s best for the child.

Want to foster a child or learn more about fostering?

Fertility struggles or being unable to conceive through traditional means can be challenging for anyone who longs to start or grow a family. But now that you’re aware of some possible pathways to parenthood, you can reflect on which route is best for you.

Fostering offers a wonderful opportunity to experience parenthood while also transforming the future of a child who needs your support. For many people facing fertility challenges, it can become a fulfilling and rewarding way to grow a family and create lasting bonds.

If you want to learn more about becoming a foster parent or have any questions about the process, download our guide, Fostering 101: The Beginner’s Guide to Fostering a Child.

You can also contact our friendly and supportive team, who will gladly answer any questions you have on 0800 023 4561 or by submitting your details via our online form.

Types of fostering

As no two children are the same, there are many different types of foster care.

View all types

Short Term Fostering

Short term fostering is caring for a child on a short term basis. However, this can be from a few nights or weeks up to a couple of years.

Short term fostering

Long Term Fostering

This type of fostering placement is usually arranged when a child cannot return to their birth family and would benefit from a single stable family environment up until adulthood.

Long term fostering

Emergency Fostering

Emergency fostering provides short term care for children and young people who are in urgent need of a safe and secure home.

Emergency fostering

Respite Fostering

Respite foster placements are very short – often just a couple of days – and are arranged to provide a break to a child’s parents or main foster family.

Respite fostering

Parent and child fostering

A type of foster placement that helps support young people who have become a parent at a young age. The foster parent’s role will be to assess and support the young parent in nurturing and raising their child.

Parent and child fostering

Step down fostering

This type of fostering is designed to help young people make the transition from residential care to a family home.

Step down fostering

Sibling Fostering

Keeping brothers and sisters together after being placed in foster care is crucial. This type of foster placement focuses on matching sibling groups with foster parents who have the space and skills to care for them.

Fostering siblings

Foster placements for disabled children

A short-term respite placement aimed to provide the carers of children with a physical, learning or sensory disability, with a short break from their responsibilities. This type of fostering can range from a few hours to a whole weekend.

Disability fostering

Fostering for sanctuary-seeking children

When a child seeks asylum in the UK without a suitable adult to care for them, a sanctuary-seeking foster placement is set up to ensure the child is safe and has access to the specialist care and support they may need while they apply for refugee status.

Fostering for sanctuary-seeking children

items.title: The Little Family We Have Become: Rosane’s First Year of Fostering
items.snippet: After celebrating her first year of fostering, Rosane reflects on how becoming a foster parent has changed her life. Discover her experience of fostering as a single parent, the support she receives from FCA, and the everyday moments that make fostering so rewarding. The post The Little Family We Have Become: Rosane’s First Year of Fostering appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
After just one year of fostering, Rosane already struggles to imagine life before it.

Alongside her grown-up daughter Rebecca, she currently cares for three children and has embraced the joys, challenges and unexpected rewards that fostering brings.

Drawing on her experience as a psychotherapist, Rosane felt called to make a difference to children who needed stability, love and support. She gives a moving account of how becoming a foster parent has truly changed her life, how she navigates fostering as a single foster parent, and the profound difference you can make to children’s lives.

 

Deciding to foster

Rosane’s decision to foster wasn’t something that happened overnight. Having spent many years supporting children and families through her professional career, she already understood the life-changing impact that a caring adult can have on a child’s future.

“I don’t see fostering as a job, it is more like a calling. I’ve always been drawn to supporting children and young people. Before becoming a foster carer, I worked for many years as a psychotherapist, helping children, families, and adults navigate difficult experiences. Throughout my career, I saw first-hand the profound difference that a safe, stable, and nurturing adult can make in a child’s life.”

Starting the journey

“I researched several fostering agencies before making my decision. FCA stood out because of its child-centred approach, comprehensive training programme, and the support available to foster carers. I wanted to feel part of an organisation that genuinely valued both children and carers, and FCA gave me that confidence from the beginning, the moment I made my initial enquiry.”

She shared more about her assessment journey:

“The assessment process was thorough, which I believe is incredibly important given the responsibility involved in fostering. But the months seemed to pass in the blink of an eye, and I genuinely enjoyed the process far more than I expected.”

“What surprised me most was how reflective and emotional parts of the journey were. The process invites you to look back at your own childhood, your life experiences, the people who shaped you, and the moments that contributed to making you the person you are today. At times, this was both challenging and moving, but it also gave me a greater understanding of myself and the values I wanted to bring into fostering.”

Are you thinking of fostering?

Download the FCA’s complete beginner’s guide to fostering a child. Find out more on how to foster a child and the process involved.

DOWNLOAD GUIDE

The difference of fostering with FCA

For Rosane, having the right support around her has made all the difference, particularly as a single foster parent who also works alongside fostering. From day one, she has felt part of a wider fostering community that is there whenever she needs advice, guidance or reassurance.

“The support I receive from FCA has been invaluable, particularly as a single foster carer. From the very beginning, I’ve felt that I am part of a team rather than doing this alone. Everyone is approachable, supportive, and genuinely invested in achieving the best outcomes for the children. Knowing that there is always someone available to offer advice, guidance, or simply a listening ear provides enormous reassurance.”

“I especially value the relationship I have with my supervising social worker. I trust her completely and know that I can reach out whenever I need advice, whether I’m navigating a challenge or simply seeking reassurance that I’m on the right track. Having that trusted relationship has helped me feel more confident in my role and has made a significant difference to my experience as a foster carer.”

“Fostering can be emotionally demanding at times, but the support network provided by FCA helps you feel understood, valued, and never alone.”

Quiet confirmation you’re making a difference

Ask most foster parents about their proudest moments and they’ll often talk about the small things rather than the big milestones. For Rosane, it’s the everyday moments that show just how far children have come and how secure they feel within her family:

“I witness special moments and milestones almost every single day. Some of the most meaningful achievements are not the big events that everyone sees, but the small everyday moments that show how far the children have come and how safe, loved, and settled they feel.”

“One moment that has always stayed with me was when my 11-year-old foster child casually said, ‘It doesn’t feel like I’m in care’. To many people, it might sound like a simple comment, but to me it meant everything. It was one of those moments that quietly confirms you’re making a difference.”

“The bedtime moments are particularly special. There is something magical about hearing ‘I love you’ before lights out, knowing that the children are going to sleep feeling safe and cared for. The school run is another favourite part of my day: Dropping them off in the morning and seeing the excitement in their eyes, knowing they feel confident enough to face the day because they know I have their back, is incredibly rewarding.”

“Then there are our family film nights, which bear very little resemblance to actually watching a film – nobody can hear a single word over the chatter, the floor is covered in popcorn, we’ve missed half the story, and we’re all laughing too much to care. To some people, it might sound like complete chaos. To us, it’s our magic chaos. It’s our way of being the little family we have become.”

“When I look back on my young fostering journey so far, it is the everyday moments of connection, belonging, laughter, and love that I treasure the most. Those moments remind me why fostering is so important and why it has become such a meaningful part of my life.”

These quiet moments of trust, belonging and connection are the ones Rosane treasures most and are a constant reminder of the difference fostering can make.

Children don’t need perfection

Rosane reflected on her first year of fostering and what she has learned from her experience: “If I had to sum up my fostering experience in one sentence, I’d say it’s the most rewarding adventure I’ve ever signed up for – and more love than I could ever have imagined. Every day is different, and while there are certainly challenges along the way, the joyful moments far outweigh them.”

“What has surprised me most is how naturally we have become a family. The children have brought so much energy, laughter, and personality into our home. Our lives are fuller, noisier, and much happier because of them.”

“One of the things that makes me smile the most is the relationship they have developed with my daughter, Rebecca. They absolutely adore their big sister and look up to her as a positive role model. Watching that sibling bond grow has been incredibly special.”

“Fostering has strengthened my belief that children don’t need perfection; they need consistency, patience, love, and someone who believes in them. Of course, fostering comes with challenges, but it has also brought immeasurable joy, love, and purpose into our lives. Watching the children grow in confidence, feel safe, begin to see their own worth, and simply enjoy being children has been one of the greatest privileges of my life.”

Fostering as a single foster parent

Many people assume fostering as a single person would be difficult, but Rosane believes it reinforces that families come in all shapes and sizes.

“Being a single foster parent has certainly brought challenges, but it has also been one of the most rewarding experiences of my life. I’ve gone from being a single parent of one to being a single parent of four – it’s multitasking on a completely different level!”

“Of course, there is no one else to share the day-to-day responsibilities, so organisation, flexibility and resilience are essential. Some days can feel like managing a small business, a taxi company, a restaurant, and a counselling service all at the same time!”

“At the same time, being a single foster parent has been incredibly empowering. I’ve learned to trust my instincts, rely on the support available to me, and create a stable, loving, and nurturing environment for the children. My daughter has also been an amazing source of support throughout our fostering journey and together we have built a home where everyone feels welcomed, valued, and cared for.”

“Like any family, we have our busy days, our funny moments, and our occasional chaos, but there is always love at the centre of it all. Being a single foster parent has shown me that families come in many different shapes and sizes, and what matters most is not how many adults are in the home, but how much care, commitment, and love the children receive.”

Download our guide to the fostering assessment

Download our free Guide to the Fostering Assessment to learn everything you need to know about becoming a foster parent — from making your first enquiry to getting approved, being matched with a child, and the support you’ll receive along the way.

Download Guide

A house becoming a home

Fostering can bring so much to your life as a foster parent and Rosane shared with us some of the things she has found most special:

“One good thing I wish I’d known before starting fostering is just how much love would come into my life. Before becoming a foster carer, I understood that I would be making a difference in children’s lives, but I never imagined how much they would change mine. These children had been through so much, yet they still found space in their hearts to trust, connect, and love me back. That is something I don’t think anyone can fully prepare you for. I could never have imagined that just one year later, I would struggle to remember what life was like before they came into it.”

“When I look at where the children were when they first arrived and compare it to where they are now, I realise that the real difference is not found in one single moment. It is found in all the small moments that have added up over time. The most powerful have been the moments when they showed that they truly felt they belonged. Watching them gradually stop seeing our house as somewhere temporary and instead refer to it as home has been incredibly moving. It is difficult to put into words what it means to witness children who once lived with uncertainty begin to feel safe, secure, and loved as part of a family.”

Don’t underestimate the difference you can make

Rosane is passionate about encouraging others to consider fostering. She believes many people underestimate the impact they could have on a child’s life and the rewards that fostering can bring in return.

She said: “Children in care don’t need perfect carers; they need caring, committed adults who are willing to be patient, consistent, and present. My advice would be not to underestimate the difference you can make. You don’t need to have all the answers. What matters most is being willing to learn, seek support, and provide a safe and nurturing environment.”

“Fostering may give you the opportunity to change a child’s life, but it also changes your own for the better – and watching a child discover their strengths, build confidence, and begin to believe that they deserve good things in life is worth all the effort.”

While fostering may begin with a desire to help a child, it often becomes a journey that changes your own life too.

 

If you want to make a difference to children by providing a loving home, please get in touch with our team to find out more about fostering.

Shortage of Scottish foster carers is a care emergency
items.snippet: A shortage of Scottish foster carers is a care emergency. TACT's Andy Elvin calls for a sector-wide integrated approach to address the issue. The post Shortage of Scottish foster carers is a care emergency appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Shortage of Scottish foster carers is a care emergency

A recent statement issued by Scotland’s thirty-two Chief Social Work Officers has highlighted an acute shortage of available fostering homes in Scotland, with children as young as three being placed in residential homes.

Whilst a shortage of foster carers across the UK has been a long-standing issue, children under five years old being placed in residential homes alongside much older young people is alarming. A local authority’s own foster carers are historically approached first to care for very young children, so with residential home placements being sought instead – this points to a general lack of foster carers across Scotland. This points to a care emergency that should be triggering an urgent ‘call to action’ for the government and fostering providers to increase carer recruitment efforts.

“We do need more action at a governmental level as a matter of urgency to bring more people to fostering across Scotland. We would happily work with our Scottish LA colleagues and the Scottish government in a national foster carer recruitment effort. It is clear that we need to work together in concert to address this emergency.”

Andy Elvin, TACT CEO

Andy Elvin, TACT CEO and Chair of The Fairer Fostering Partnership, said: “With the recent statement issued by Scotland’s thirty-two Chief Social Work Officers with regards to the acute shortage of available fostering homes, it is clear that this is a care emergency. Children as young as three being placed in residential homes isn’t acceptable or in the best interests of children.

“Here at TACT, we’ve introduced a number of financial wellbeing initiatives to help make fostering viable for more people. We’ve also introduced our ‘making spaces’ program centred around increasing our carers’ spare bedroom capacity to provide additional care, particularly to help bring siblings together.

“However, we do need more action at a governmental level as a matter of urgency to bring more people to fostering across Scotland. We would happily work with our Scottish LA colleagues and the Scottish government in a national foster carer recruitment effort. It is clear that we need to work together in concert to address this emergency. The new legislation requiring that all Independent Fostering Providers are charities is an excellent opportunity to promote fostering across Scotland.”

So what can be done? The initial response needs to be focused on finding suitable foster homes for those under fives that are being placed in residential homes. Providing care for young people with complex needs has also been highlighted as a priority. Local authorities would need to prioritise their own recruitment strategies, of course. Independent fostering agencies based in, or covering Scotland, should not only formulate integrated carer recruitment marketing campaigns aimed at providing care for the under fives – they should be looking to nurture and upskill their current foster carers, where possible.

Moving forward, there does need to be a general change in the way local authorities approach the referral and matching process for under fives and, in fact, all young people.

All referrals for foster care should call on both in-house local authority carers and external agency carers simultaneously – with the ‘best match’ being the goal in every single scenario. With a level playing field of care requests, all fostering providers would be in a better position to respond to care emergencies such as this. Ultimately it would help to create a wider pool of skilled foster carers able to care for children of all ages and with differing needs.

Read more about fostering in Scotland with TACT.

items.title: Need for more ‘under 5’ foster carers in Scotland
items.snippet: There is an urgent need for more foster carers in Scotland to provide care for children under five years old. Why is this? The post Need for more ‘under 5’ foster carers in Scotland appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Need for more ‘under 5’ foster carers in Scotland

Does the need for more foster carers to care for babies and ‘under 5’ children in Scotland point to a reduced pool of foster carers, more children coming into care – or are there more complex reasons?

It is an expected scenario that very young children are usually placed with a local authority’s own foster carers, with older children, or those with more complex needs, being referred to independent fostering agencies. However, since January 2026, 41% of TACT’s referrals from across Scotland have been for children aged under five. This has represented a significant shift in the age bracket of children being referred externally to fostering agencies.

There could be many reasons for this, and it is difficult to pinpoint any single factor. Let’s look at two most likely causes, what can be done – and what needs to change.

General decrease in foster carers in Scotland

Whilst it is difficult to access up-to-date statistics from other organisations, Plan 24-30 reported that between 2019 and 2024 the number of registered fostering households decreased by 21.8% in Scotland. Reasons for this are not easily identifiable, but could point to foster carers naturally retiring from the sector versus a decline in the number of new fostering households coming forward. In addition, budgets for carer recruitment marketing campaigns could be squeezed, reducing the active push for new carers.

The number of children and young people requiring care also fell during this period, but the number of available foster carers declined at a faster rate.

A reduced pool of foster carers across Scottish local authorities will, of course, result in those referrals for very young children being pushed out to external agencies.

But there lies our next problem.

External fostering agency carers not prepared for ‘under 5’s’

Many independent fostering agencies recruit their foster carers based on the traditional construct of providing care for older children, with those solely wishing to care for under fives being signposted to their local authority.

The reason why some foster carers may not be able to provide care for younger children could be that it does not fit their current household composition, skill set or preference. They would also need to be approved by a fostering panel to provide care for that age group.

Fostering infants and toddlers presents different challenges from fostering older children, as carers must provide highly responsive care that meets young children’s developmental, emotional, and health needs during the very important stage of early growth.

If external agency foster carers are not prepared to provide matched foster care for under fives, because they were never expected to, this could create an impasse if local authorities don’t have enough foster carers generally.

What can Fostering Providers do?

As a fostering charity, TACT will always aim to prioritise certain foster carer recruitment based on a demand for a specific type of fostering per region, alongside a more general recruitment push.

As previously mentioned, a focus on recruiting carers to provide care for under fives would usually be off the table for independent fostering agencies – but it is clear that this is not the case in Scotland. Local authorities would need to prioritise their own recruitment strategies, of course. Independent fostering agencies based in, or covering Scotland, should not only formulate integrated carer recruitment marketing campaigns aimed at providing care for the under fives – they should be looking to nurture and upskill their current foster carers, where possible.

As a charitable fostering agency, TACT’s focus has always been on the wider care system and great outcomes for children, over and above profit or traditional business focuses. By actioning specific carer recruitment and nurturing strategies, the sector would be providing a workable plan to help create a natural influx of foster carers able to provide care for the under fives in Scotland; a ‘call to arms’ outside of any one organisations’ own interests.

What needs to change?

Moving forward, there does need to be a general change in the way local authorities approach the referral and matching process for under fives and, in fact, all young people.

Referrals should call on both in-house local authority carers and external agency carers simultaneously – with the ‘best match’ being the goal in every single scenario. If more external agencies were to receive referrals for very young children, they would adapt their recruitment strategies to match demand. As it stands, there is a potential block when it comes to recruiting carers for under fives, because these referrals are traditionally pushed to local authority carers first.

This has been an historic issue for many years, and it does need to change. With a level playing field, children will not only benefit from the best match across their local authority and external agencies, it will also help create a wider pool of skilled foster carers able to care for children of all ages.

Read more about Fostering in Scotland with TACT.

The post Need for more ‘under 5’ foster carers in Scotland appeared first on TACT.

items.title: Tips to Make Your Foster Child’s Birthday Special
items.snippet: Celebrating a foster child’s birthday is a chance to create joyful, lasting memories. With thoughtful planning and care, you can make their day feel truly special and meaningful. Explore simple yet impactful tips to help ensure your foster child feels valued, celebrated, and happy on their big day. The post Tips to Make Your Foster Child’s Birthday Special appeared first on Orange Grove Foster Care.
items.content:
Caring for a foster child means providing a loving, comfortable home every single day. It also means making the most of special occasions, particularly your foster child’s birthday. Just because they can’t spend it with their birth family doesn’t mean that they have to miss out on a memory they can cherish forever.

Birthdays with a foster child are so important. Your foster child may not have had a positive birthday before, so it’s up to you to provide them with memories to last a lifetime. The good news is that we’ve put together a list of 8 tips to help you make this a birthday they’ll never forget.

Let’s take a look at how you can make your foster child’s birthday special.

Giving your foster children emotional support

Although it’s easy to get swept up in the excitement of birthdays and a family gathering, it’s crucial to bear the needs and feelings of your foster child in mind. Birthdays could also be a triggering occasion that reminds them they’re not able to spend this time with their birth family, so it’s a time that needs compassion and empathy.

The most important thing to bear in mind when you’re thinking about how to make a foster child’s birthday special is to talk to them about what they want. Listen to them if they ask you not to include something, or think of a suitable alternative that you think they would appreciate.

Managing your expectations will also be key throughout the planning process and the day itself. They might be overwhelmed and not think to thank you for your hard work. Or you may need to help them express their emotions in a healthy way if there’s an aspect of the day that they struggle with.

8 tips to give your foster child a memorable birthday

 

Give them a Thoughtful Gift

The most important thing to remember is to get your foster child a thoughtful gift that you know they’ll love. Spend some time thinking carefully about what they would want for their birthday, or if you’re unsure, you can always ask them if there’s anything they would like. This will depend on their age, interests, and preference, and should be age appropriate.

To make sure that your foster child can have a wonderful birthday, we give all our foster parents an additional foster care payment to cover birthday budgets. Here at Orange Grove Foster Care, we provide a £100 annual birthday allowance to ensure you can give your foster child the birthday that they deserve.

Be mindful of the fact that presents might not bring them joy in the way you intended, too. It might cause some children to feel guilty that their parents couldn’t offer them the same generosity. The gift you choose to give them doesn’t have to be something expensive – a small gesture would be just as thoughtful as something more extravagant.

Another thing to consider is that they may not know how to react when given a gift. Some children may have only experienced gifts with the expectation that they must give the gift-giver something in return. Reassure them that this isn’t the case if they seem unsure of how to behave.

Get the Whole Family Involved

Show your foster child how special they are by making their birthday a family affair. Invite the grandparents, aunties, uncles, and cousins for a get-together that they will remember forever. Not only will fun memories get made, but they might also receive extra presents.

If your foster child is in school and has friends of their own you could invite, you can include them, too. This could give them something else to look forward to if people they know and love are able to come along and share in the celebrations.

Before you make any concrete plans, talk to your foster child about how many people they want over, or if they want anyone over at all. Some children prefer a quieter affair, or might not want a fuss. You don’t want to overwhelm them if they’d prefer to avoid having loads of people around. Some children could find large gatherings overwhelming, and it might serve to remind them of who isn’t there for their birthday.

If they’re unsure about having lots of people over, show them that they’re loved by getting everyone to sign a birthday card for them instead. Siblings could make a card for them to show that they care, or help you to cook a special meal for your foster child instead.

Take them on a Trip

Birthdays are the perfect opportunity for a fun trip. Ask your foster child if there’s something they would love to do for their birthday. Or if there’s something that they’ve been talking about doing or somewhere they’ve been wanting to visit for a while, this gives you the ideal chance to do just that. No matter what you choose to do, as long as it’s something your foster child will love, it’ll be an unforgettable experience.

Make sure that whatever you decide to do is age-appropriate for your foster child’s interests, whether you’re fostering teenagers or younger children.

Not sure what to do? Here are a few ideas:

  • Beach trip
  • Birthday barbecue in the park
  • Shopping spree
  • Theme park
  • Museum
  • Zoo or aquarium
  • Birthday meal at their favourite restaurant

Work on a Birthday Project Together

Another fantastic way to make memories that you and your foster child can cherish forever is to work on a project together. This is an excellent way to make something tangible to remember each other by, especially if it’s something that your foster child particularly enjoys doing, such as crafts.

Here are a few suggestions of what you could work on together:

  • Bake a cake together and let them choose their favourite recipe
  • Create a scrapbook of your time together
  • Get creative with drawings
  • Design a puppet theatre they can play with
  • Make beaded bracelets they can wear, or get them to make friendship bracelets with friends

Support Contact with Birth Parents

Part of your role as a foster parent will be to support contact with birth parents. Birthdays are typically a time when your foster child can get in touch with their birth family, and this often requires comfort and understanding. It’s important to bear in mind that emotions can run high, with excitement, worry, and fear becoming overwhelming for some.

An important thing to consider is that you may need to manage your foster child’s disappointment if they don’t get the reaction they hoped for from their birth parents. The parents might not mark their birthday in the way they wanted, or they might forget that it’s their birthday at all. Help your foster child to understand that it isn’t because they’re not worth loving, and show them that they deserve to feel loved and cared for.

You may notice a change in the behaviour of your foster child around this time because of their complex emotions around contacting their birth family. Be as understanding and patient with them as you can as they process their feelings, and allow them to talk to you about it. Validate their feelings and reassure them that they’re loved. However, if they’d rather not talk about it, then don’t push them to do so.

Let Them Blow Out Their Candles

Unfortunately, some foster children never get a chance to blow out their birthday cake candles. Whether that is or isn’t the case for your foster child, let them blow out their candles on their birthday.

They might never have experienced a traditional birthday that included something as simple as this or even having a cake to celebrate them, so this could be a poignant memory for them to cherish.

Ensure that the attention is solely on them when the cake is being brought out, and everyone is singing happy birthday. Today is their special day, and it’s important that they know it’s all about them.

Remember to tell them to make a wish, too!

Don’t Hold Any Expectations

You might start the day imagining how amazing it’s going to be, and how thankful your foster child will be when they see how much effort you’ve put into their special day.

However, it’s key to remember that most foster children will never have experienced a birthday in the way others have, and the whole experience may be overwhelming at first. This could manifest in strong emotions throughout the day, so you’ll need to treat them with empathy and understanding.

Another thing to consider is that you might not get a thank you in return for your hard work, particularly if your foster child is processing complex feelings.

Don’t hold any expectations about how your foster child will react to their birthday presents and surprises. If you sense that they are overwhelmed, do what you can to release pressure. You can create a code word together before the event that your foster child can use to tell you that they’re feeling overwhelmed and need some space. Make sure they know that they don’t have to do anything they don’t want to during their birthday.

Talk to your Foster Child About What They Want

The best way to ensure that your foster child experiences the best birthday ever is to sit down and ask them what they want. That’s the only way you’ll determine how to make their birthday the occasion they hope it will be.

Your foster child will appreciate you taking the time to consider what they want for their birthday. If they want to have lots of friends around, or if they want a quieter day where it’s just a small handful of people, taking these preferences into consideration will make the day even better for them.

Supporting foster children on birthdays

As much as we love celebrating the birthdays of loved ones, it’s important to remember that this might be a difficult time for your foster child, particularly if they’re unable to spend their birthday with their birth family. Showing compassion will be crucial to helping them work through their feelings during this time, and taking a trauma-informed approach when they become dysregulated and show big emotions.

Here are a few of our top tips for helping them to navigate their feelings:

  • Create a safe space – give your foster children the opportunity to talk about how they feel, and validate their emotions. Talking to a trusted adult is an important part of their healing process.
  • Stay calm – when they become dysregulated, stay calm and keep your body language relaxed and open. This can help them to regulate their own emotions.
  • Listen to their preferences – we know you mean well by wanting to give them the best birthday ever. But if they appear uncomfortable about these plans, then it’s important to listen to them and accommodate what they want to do for their birthday, even if that’s simply time spent quietly in the home or working on a hobby.

items.title: Sarah First Year Reflections
items.snippet: Over the past year, Sarah has welcomed children into her home and focused on building strong, trusting relationships, supported by her wider network and her dog, Gertie, who plays a special role in helping children feel safe and settled. The post Sarah First Year Reflections appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
Deciding to foster is a big step, and the first year in particular is a period of significant learning, growth, and connection. It brings a mix of new experiences, meaningful moments, and important milestones. It is the small, everyday interactions that often leave the biggest impact; building trust, creating routines, and forming bonds that matter. This first year is not just about change, but about laying the foundations for something truly meaningful, making fostering a journey well worth celebrating.

Sarah, one of our Midlands foster carers, has recently celebrated her first-year milestone in her fostering journey.

Over the past year, Sarah has welcomed children into her home and focused on building strong, trusting relationships, supported by her wider network and her dog, Gertie, who plays a special role in helping children feel safe and settled.

As she reflects on this first year, Sarah shares some of the moments that have shaped her journey as a foster carer with Swiis.

Looking back on your first year of fostering with Swiis, how would you describe the experience?

“Looking back on my first year of fostering, it has been a real learning journey. I have gained a much deeper understanding of how important clear boundaries are, and how they help create stability and safety for children in my care. Like many new foster carers, I learned a lot through experience, and those lessons have helped me grow in confidence and approach each care arrangement with greater clarity.”

“My first arrangement helped me understand just how resilient children and young people can be, even after experiencing significant challenges in their lives. Building trust took time, but when those moments of connection came, they felt incredibly meaningful.”

As a single foster carer, what has your experience been like, and what have you found most rewarding about fostering on your own?

“Fostering as a single carer has had its challenges, but it has also brought many positives. While there are moments when I need to pause and reflect on situations independently, I have learned how to process things calmly and confidently.”

“I am fortunate to have a supportive network around me, including my daughter and close friends, who I can talk things through with when needed.”

“Having that one-to-one time with the child in my care has helped us build strong bonds and develop trusting relationships.”

Can you share the types of support you received during your first year of fostering with Swiis, and how this support made a difference for you?

“The support I have received from my supervising social worker has been invaluable throughout my first year of fostering. Whenever I have had concerns or felt unsure about certain behaviours, she has been quick to respond, sharing helpful guidance and reassurance.”

“This guidance has supported my learning and helped me move forward with confidence and a more informed approach.”

“Jordon Murdoch, the stability and support manager has also been a lifesaver, offering practical advice and reassurance around managing different behaviours as they arise. I have also felt well supported by the out of hours service, which has given me real peace of mind.”

“All of this support has helped me feel part of a wider network that is there to guide, encourage, and support me to achieve the best possible outcomes for the child in my care.”

Your dog Gertie is such an important part of your home. How has she helped children feel more settled and comfortable?

“My dog Gertie has been remarkable with the children who come into my home. From the very beginning, they have felt safe and comfortable around her. She shows them so much love and affection which always helps bring out the best in them.”

“Animals can be a wonderful tool to help children learn empathy and gentleness and this has extended to other animals in the home too.”

“At one point I had ten chickens, which needed to be handled very carefully and this helped the children understand the importance of treating animals with compassion. When they show that care and kindness, they are rewarded with trust and show us lots of love in return, which was lovely to see.”

Can you share a particularly memorable experience from your first year of fostering with Swiis?

“There have been many positive moments that have stayed with me during my first year of fostering. When my first child began to open up and share her feelings, that was incredibly meaningful. Knowing that she trusted me enough to do so showed how far she had come and how safe she felt in my care.”

“My second child is full of energy. Every hug he gives me is memorable, as he means every squeeze, and those moments are a powerful reminder of the positive impact fostering can have.”

What advice or tips would you give to someone considering fostering as a single carer?

“I would highly recommend fostering to anyone who wants to make a genuine difference in a child’s life. I wish I would have done this years ago!”

“For single carers, having a good support network is really important, and with the right support behind you, fostering can be an incredibly positive and rewarding experience.”

Sarah’s first year with Swiis has been a journey of learning, growth and meaningful connection, she has felt supported and has asked for guidance when needed.  What a great first year, very well-done Sarah, we look forward to supporting you for many years to come.

If this story has inspired you to explore fostering, or if you would like to find out more about becoming a foster carer, contact our recruitment team. They will be happy to guide you through the fostering process, explain the support, training and allowances available, and answer any questions you may have.

The post Sarah First Year Reflections appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.

items.title: Going the Extra Mile Together
items.snippet: Over the weekend of 13th–14th June, FCA and FCA Scotland came together for the annual “Going the Extra Mile” event, uniting foster families, children, young people, and staff in a shared challenge that went far beyond its 3,155-mile target. With over 3,200 miles completed through walks, runs, rides, and adventurous activities, the weekend was a powerful celebration of connection, community, and support across the FCA fostering family. The post Going the Extra Mile Together appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
Over the weekend of the 13th–14th June, foster parents, children, young people and staff from across FCA and FCA Scotland came together for our Going the Extra Mile event and what an incredible weekend it was!

This year, we had an ambitious aim to cover 3155 miles which symbolised one mile for every foster family, every child who fosters and every child we care for to show that no one at FCA walks alone.

AND WE DID IT!!

Together, we achieved an incredible 3200.58 miles (over 5150 km!) proving once again that when we come together, we really can go the extra mile.

We certainly covered those miles in style! From horse riding and dog walks to scootering, colour runs, sailing, mud runs, cycling and even an ultra marathon, there were so many fantastic ways for everyone to get involved. Whether taking on personal challenges, enjoying family adventures or joining colleagues and friends, every mile counted.

We also raised money for Fin, also known as The Mighty Fin, thanks to April Newman from FCA Cymru. Fin lives with a very rare, life-limiting condition called Mowat-Wilson Syndrome, which has affected virtually all aspects of his development. Despite this, Fin’s outlook is nothing short of inspiring and it was a privilege for our community to support such an incredible boy and his family.

Going the Extra Mile was a wonderful reminder of the power of community. FCA is huge, spread across many regions, but what makes weekends like this so special is how they bring us all together. No matter where we are, we are united by one shared goal, to support children, young people and each other.

Events like this remind us that although we may be miles apart day to day, we are always connected as one fostering family.

A huge thank you to everyone who took part and helped make the weekend such a success. Every step, pedal, bounce and stride contributed to something truly special, and together, we showed that at FCA, no one walks alone.

Together, we went the extra mile.

items.title: A Wake-Up Call: Supporting Care-Experienced Young People into Work
items.snippet: NEET is a growing national challenge. TACT's Sian Biddlecombe and Sam Gray identify what is potentially driving the crisis, and what needs to be done. The post A Wake-Up Call: Supporting Care-Experienced Young People into Work appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
A Wake-Up Call: Supporting Care-Experienced Young People into Work

At the end of May 2026, the Department for Education published its Young People & Work Interim Report, shining a stark light on a growing national challenge: almost one million young people aged 16–24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training (NEET).

While the overall NEET rate for young people is 13.5%, this rises dramatically to 40% for care-experienced young people aged 19–21. This is not just concerning, it is a national crisis.

Behind these statistics are complex realities. Around 60% of young people who are NEET are economically inactive, meaning they are not currently seeking work. Even more striking, 60% have never had a job, despite 84% saying they want to work. This clearly shows that this is not about a lack of motivation – it is about barriers.

What is driving the NEET crisis?

The report highlights several key factors:

  • Health and wellbeing challenges: Rising levels of mental health needs and neurodevelopmental conditions are now a primary driver of young people becoming disconnected from work.
  • A changing labour market: Entry-level roles have declined, recruitment is increasingly automated, and apprenticeships have fallen by 40%.
  • Employer expectations: Many employers are seeking prior experience even for entry-level roles, alongside concerns about providing pastoral support.
  • Cuts to early intervention and prevention services: Reductions in funding across early years, SEND provision, youth services, and Further Education have reduced the support available to young people.
  • System barriers: 1 in 10 under-19s do not complete their course and 1 in 6 do not achieve a Level 3 qualification.
  • Practical barriers: lack of transport, housing costs, childcare, and even the upfront cost of uniforms or equipment can all prevent young people from taking their first steps into employment.

Why are care-experienced young people most affected?

For children and young people in care, these challenges are often intensified; disrupted education due to placement or school moves at critical stages, unmet support for children with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), and limited exposure to careers education and opportunities can all play a part.

If there are gaps in a young person’s Pathway Plan – a document that maps out a transition to independent living – this .can also make young people vulnerable, particularly if there is also delayed access to Personal Advisers.

There are also wider social impacts; loneliness among young people has surged since 2019, with 1 in 5 young adults having one or no close friends. Without strong social networks, access to opportunities becomes even harder. Lower aspirations due to a lack of visible role models is another potential factor.

As one quote from the report captures powerfully: “The opportunities might be there, but if no one in your immediate family or social circle does that sort of thing, you haven’t seen it – so you don’t believe you can be it.”

“The issue has an impact on confidence, independence, health, and future life chances.  Care-experienced young people have ambitions, talent, and potential. They want to work. Our role as professionals, carers, partners and communities is to ensure that the pathways are there, the support is in place, and the belief is built.  Every young person deserves the chance to see a future and to achieve it.”

Sian Biddlecombe, TACT’s Head of Education

How TACT’s Education Service is helping to tackle NEET

As a charity who has established their own Education and Health Services, along with a care-experienced community called Connect, TACT have already put in place a number of initiatives:

  • Early intervention and support from our qualified advisors: for our social workers, foster carers and young people when education placements are not meeting needs or when exclusions arise.
  • Investing in potential and growing passions: we use our aspirational funding and education funding to provide a range of experiences and opportunities – from music lessons and sports clubs to school trips abroad, right through to mentoring, tuition, books and tickets to theatre, sporting and cultural events.
  • Practical employability support: including revision skills, CV writing, applications and interview preparation with our Post-16 team.
  • Access to help and support with pathway planning: such as the Apprenticeship Academy course or UCAS application support.
  • TACT Connect, offering lifelong community and support: as well as continued access to our Post-16 advisors for help with employment and education issues.
  • Partnership working: with organisations such as Springpod, NNECL, Become and the Rees Foundation to expand access to work experience, mentoring and careers networks.
  • Access to mental health support and assessments via TACT’s Health Service.

NEET: What more needs to be done?

Whilst we are proud of the work we have already done here at TACT, there is always more to do. Early intervention is key, such as starting careers education earlier and then embedding careers conversations across all communications with young people. Identifying young people at risk of becoming NEET sooner would mean strategies could be put in place.

Employers would need to play their part too; employer engagement and access to work experience and real-world opportunities would help further down the line.

However, it is not simply about employment. The issue has an impact on confidence, independence, health, and future life chances.  Care-experienced young people have ambitions, talent, and potential. They want to work. Our role as professionals, carers, partners and communities is to ensure that the pathways are there, the support is in place, and the belief is built.  Every young person deserves the chance to see a future and to achieve it.

Sian Biddlecombe (Head of Education) and Sam Gray (Post-16 Advisor)

Read more about TACT’s Education Service.

Legoland Visit Builds Long Lasting Friendships
items.snippet: Our South West team treated our fostering households to a trip to Legoland, which proved invaluable way beyond the activities and attractions! The post Legoland Visit Builds Long Lasting Friendships appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Legoland Visit Builds Long Lasting Friendships

Our brilliant TACT South West team took 60 of our fostering families to Legoland Windsor – but it wasn’t just the rides and attractions that everyone enjoyed.

During the May half-term holiday, the South-West team enjoyed a fantastic day out at Legoland Windsor Resort with more than 60 foster families! Families travelled together by coach from Bristol, while others met us at the park, ready for a fun-filled day of adventure. Once inside, everyone set off to explore the attractions, and throughout the day we enjoyed catching up with families as we wandered around the park. 

We came back together at lunchtime to share stories about the rides and attractions everyone had experienced. One of the highlights of the day was seeing families able to bring along members of their wider support networks, creating an opportunity for everyone to enjoy the day together. It was also wonderful to see young people who had met at previous events spending time together and strengthening their friendships. 

We had overwhelmingly positive feedback from both foster carers and young people who said how fantastic the day had been, and especially how valuable it was to include those wider support networks. The opportunity the day provided for people to connect with others and build long-lasting friendships was invaluable.

A big thank you to our South West team for organising this wonderful trip! It truly shows the value of our wellbeing days; providing opportunities for our fostering households to come together, and for friendships to be nurtured and strengthened.

items.title: Stories of the Perfect Match: How the Right Pairing Changes Lives
items.snippet: A strong match between foster carers and children can make a lasting difference. Explore real-life fostering success stories and see how thoughtful matching helps build trust, improve outcomes, and create brighter futures for children in care and the families who support them. The post Stories of the Perfect Match: How the Right Pairing Changes Lives appeared first on Fosterplus.
items.content:
At Fosterplus, we know the importance of a good match. That’s why our dedicated referrals team works hard to make sure that we’ve matched children with foster parents who are the best fit for them. A good match can be the difference these children need for positive outcomes, allowing them to build brighter futures for themselves.

We’re taking a look at some real-life successful foster care stories so that you can see for yourself how matching really makes a difference. Fostering can be a hard job at times, but seeing how you actively change lives makes this one of the most rewarding vocations you can do.

Each of these positive fostering experiences was made possible because of the great care we take in the matching process. You can find more stories about fostering teenagers and other case studies on our blog.

Erin’s Story

Erin found her foster family through Fosterplus and has become part of the family since she was first matched with them.

She said, “The day I moved in, Mum had got me a little pink cake covered in butterflies that said, ‘Welcome to the Family’ on it. I’ve still got the picture of me holding it. I started calling her my Mum, unprompted, very soon after I first moved in. To me, Mum has always been my Mum, and I’ll always be her child.”

The support and care that Erin’s Mum and family have shown her has given her the loving home that she deserves. Even though Erin is now in university, she still comes home to spend weekends with her family as part of a ‘Staying Put’ arrangement, which sees children staying with their foster families after 18 years of age to help them adjust to independence.

She said: “My foster family are my family, and the ‘Staying Put’ arrangement has given me the best of both worlds.”

Adam’s Story

Adam found his foster parents through Fosterplus at the age of 12, and has said that he didn’t feel like he’d known a good home until he was with them. Now at the age of 18, Adam’s foster parents are helping him transition to independence.

Adam said, “It was just about me not finding the right ones. I just didn’t trust people. This placement is the best one. In this family, I don’t have to keep my guard up, and I can let my walls down. I call my foster carers Mum and Dad because they were the people that taught me how to let my guard down, and they made me feel quite safe, that I didn’t have to be nervous or cautious around them.”

“I started calling them Mum and Dad about two years ago. It just sort of slipped out, and then I just kept saying it, because it feels natural and comfortable to call them that.”

Currently studying construction in college, Adam also has a job and enjoys playing guitar and socialising with his friends in his spare time.

Adam said, “I was well matched with my foster parents. I needed someone with a strong will who could help support me. I believe I was incredibly lucky to be matched with my parents.”

How does the right pairing change lives?

Children may have entered foster care for a variety of reasons. No matter why they came into care, every child deserves a loving home where they can feel safe and secure.

Here at Fosterplus, we believe that the right match can change lives for the better, no matter the length of time a foster child stays with a foster parent. Whether that’s short-term, long-term, respite foster care, or through staying put foster placements.

 

Offering a child a loving home with the right foster parents can:

  • Give them the confidence they need to build a brighter future, as well as the resilience they’ll need through life to bounce back from challenges.
  • Ensure that they complete full-time education and can focus on being a child.
  • Mean that a sibling group gets to stay together, reducing the trauma that they might experience from being removed from everything they know. Siblings who are able to stay together are more likely to have positive outcomes in life than if they were separated into different foster homes.
  • Give them the life skills that they need to thrive in the world when it comes time to leave foster care.
  • Help them to develop a sense of belonging, no matter the length of time they stay with their foster parents. Most children often stay in contact with their carers well into adulthood.

Choosing to foster with Fosterplus not only means you can make a difference in a child’s life, but you’ll also have our full support behind you so that you can do an amazing job. Some of the benefits to fostering with us include:

  • Generous fostering payments
  • Access to a 24/7 helpline
  • A dedicated supervising social worker
  • Training and development tailored to your needs and interests
  • Events for all the family
  • Rewards and discounts via our Exchange platform

Are you ready to start your fostering journey?
